WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Danish Royal Family.—Queen Alexandra's re- sernbl lace to her mother the late Queen of Denmark used frequently to be commented upon, but few seem to observe the likeness between the Queen and her father which grows more and more striking' as the years roll on. Her Majesty has King Christian's beautiful, sym- pathetic eyes, and the same gracious, gentle manner which has so endeared him to his subjects, When in Denmark the Queen spends every available moment with the aged King, walking and driving with him, and when the weather permits, picnics and fishing expedi- tions are greatly indulged in by the Royal family party. To find oneself in the presence of the King, or any member of the Danish Royal Family, when on a shopp- ing expedition in Copenhagen, is no uncommon event, for their is no mobbing, or rude staring, on the part of the Danish people.and the Royal personages move about freely, and without restraint of any kind. Princess Patricia of Connaught.—According to pre- sent arrangements, the Duke and Duchess cit Connaught and Princess Patricia, will attend the wedding of the young Duke of Saxe Coburg Gotha, which takes place on the 18th October. The Hereditary Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz will also be present at the cere- mony, and there is considerable speculation, as to a possible marriage between the Grand Duke and Princess Patricia. Duke Adolph Frederick is a lieutenant in the Ist TJhlan Guards Regiment, and four years the senior of the Princess. Moreover he is a Lutheran, and the Princess—if she married him, would not be called upon to change her religion a procedure to which Her Royal Highness is understood to be decidedly averse. The Duke of Devonshire's Irish Seat.—The Duchess of Devonshire, who has been taking the baths and waters at Aix-les-Bains, will spend part of the autumn at Lismore Castle, the Duke's beautiful seat in Ireland. Part of the Lismore estate has been recently sold, to the tenantry, but this will not affect the property as a ducal residence. The Castle' which dates from the year 1181, at one time belonged to Sir Walter Raleigh, and came into the Cavendish family in 1748—when Lady Charlottee Boyle married the fourth Duke of Devon- shire, and the estate went with her. The Castie was practically rebuilt in 1814, and was added to as recently as 1856. The Douglas Scotts.—The Duke of Buccleuch, who celebrated his seventy-fourth birthday last week, is, next to the Duke of Sutherland, the largest landowner in the United Kingdom. He has some 460,000 acres to his name, but though this is not much more than a third of the Duke of Sutherland's, his rentroll is the larger of the two, and the Duke of Buccleuch has no fewer than six magnificent country seats—one of which, Drumlanrig Castle, competes with Gordon Castle as being the lat gest i house n Scotland. The Duke is the lineal descendant of the Royal Stuarts, through the Duke of Monmouth, son of Charles 11., but he has nephews who half derive from Oliver Cromwell. These are the sons of his late brother, Lord Walter Montagu Douglas Scott, who married the daughter of the late Sir Edmund Cradock Hartopp, a descendant of Mrs. Fleetaood, who was a daughter of the Lord Protector. There is thus the singular fact of the Duke of Buccleuch's near relatives being equally descended from Charles I. and the man who brought him to execution. Women who Shoot.—The Duchess of Bedford is well- known to be one of the best lady shots in the country, and some astonishing accounts have appeared of her prowess with the gun. These credit her with a total of 3,427 head of game in one season, which must surely be a record for a single gun. The driving of game of course dispenses with the fatigue of hard walking, and with improved weapons, and smokeless powder, much in modern sport is no doubt mechanical, but the Duchess of Bedford goes in regularly for snipe, and wild duck shooting, which must be followed for the sport, rather than for the bag. She was a Miss Mary Tribe, a younger daughter of the Archdeacon of Lahore, and never fired a shot until after her marriage, some seventeen or eighteen years ago. The Duchess of Newcastle is the only other lady of ducal rank who could hold her own with the gun, with the Duchess of Bedford, but there are many first rate shots, amongst women of title. Lady Ereadalbane Lady Vivian, Lady Stewart-Richardson, and the newly-married Lady Loch, are all crack shots, whilst amongst other lovers of the gun may be mentioned Mrs. Asquith, Mrs. Alan Gardner and Mrs. George Cornwallis West. The Prohibitive Price of Furs.—The best kind of furs will be more costly than ever this season, but that is not of great moment to the great majority of us, as the fashionable and expensive kinds of furs have already soared to such heights in costliness as to be beyond the reach of any but millionaires. Whilst the millionaires have been increasing in number, the crettures which I supply the most costly kinds of furs such as the silver fox, the black fox, Russian sable and chinchilla, seeml to be disappearing,and such is the competition for their' skins, that almost any price is obtained for them. Most of tho serviceable furs however, are now so closely imitated by the preparation and dressing of other skins as to be indistinguishable to all but the expert. They also, are expensive, but they do not run into a fortune as may easily be expended upon an outfit in real furs. Moleskin, now much more expensive than it used to be will again be much in evidence this winter, especially i for long flat stoles which are to be worn thrown over the shoulder. An Old-World Fabric.—Cashmere is to have a great vogue this autumn and winter, and the trimming which appears on many of the best models consists of a simple quilling of taffeta, and embroidered buttons, in a colour exactly matching the cashmere. It is possible to obtain the new cashmeres in every possible shade, but the colours in which they look their best are dark grey, dark purfde, bronze green, beaver brown, soft pale blue, cream and white. Cashmere drapes exquisitely and in the matter of wear, few fabrics can compare with it. Fashions for Brides and Bridesmaids.—As to whether or not the bridesmaid in a wreath and veil—the latter worn off the face of course—should be numbered as one of the hatless persuasion, is a vexed question at the moment, and the majority of" maids" preferring to be on the safe side—are substituting the mob cap, or the picture hat. For quitesmall maidens, Juliet caps made of tiny flowers, or Dutch bonnets, are the favourite wear, the little people usually carrying floral crooks. For groan-up bridesmaids, the floral fan has greatly taken the place of the shower bouquet, and sheaves of lilies are enjoying a great vogue among Society brides. Lace veils have been little seen of lats, and apparently it has—at length—dawned upon prospective brides that a plain tulle or net veil is not only infinitely more becoming, but very much more comfortable wear. The Thorny Path of Literiture.—The suicide of Miss Allenby, the Lancashire teacher and authoress, is a very sad incident, but it is by no means the first of its kind that has occurred, and no doubt many of our great writers would have taken their own lives, if they had been as sensitive and as easily discouraged, as was this lady. At the present moment there are thousands of persons who are fully persuaded that they have written the finest novel of. modern times, and in some few instances there is undoubtedly good work—equal to many successful novels, of our day—which the writers cannot get published. But as a rule, the work is mediocre, although the author with limited powers of criticism considers It of surpassing excellence. In other cases the writer has read a book by some successful author,and has formed the opinion that he or she could do better. Quite likely he could, but the successful author is already known, and publishers will accept the M.S. of a known writer when they will refuse even to look at that of one who is unknown. The fate of Miss Allanby should be a warning to others not to be too ready to enter upon the thorny path of literature. The writing of Bevels. short stories, and poems, may be a very delightful rscreation to many, but when they depend upon it for their bread and butter, the case is very different.
MIDGE.

COMMERCIAL FAlLURES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of Commercial Failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, September Sth, was 140, viz. : New bankruptcy proceedings published in the London Gazette, TR; deeds of arrangement registered, 64. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were: Bankruptcies, 62; deeds of arrangement 66—total 123; being an increase of 11'. The total number of commercial failures recorded during the 36 weeks of the present year is 6,173 : the total number recorded in the corresponding 33 weeks of last year-was 6,156 showing an increase of 17.

div.head: RUNCORN PASSIVE RESISTERS.
div.p: RUNCORN PASSIVE RESISTERS.

At Runcorn on Monday, the following gentlemen were summoned for non-payment of the education portion of the poor-rate :—The Revs. H. S. Targett and T. S. Morris: Messrs. John Robert Frith, George W. Littler Robert Harold Posnett, James M. Frith. and Charles Lloyd. Only Mr. Targett appeared, and said his objection was a conscientious one, lie could not conscientiously pay the sectarian portion of the rate. An order for immediate payment was made in each case.

div.head: WOMAN'S REALM.
div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
PRINCESS GUSTAVUS OF SWEDEN.

Princess Gustavus of Sweden has been well and happy in her new home, So!Sere, the home given to her with such thoughtful kindness by King Oscar of Sweden, who spent an ideally happy married life himself there. The house has been refurnished, and many are the English books and pictures that have found their way into the Princess's pretty rooms. Nothing could have been more cordial than the reception oê our Princess Margaret in Sweden. The people are proud of her popularity in England, of her attractive presence and amiability, and they admire her pluck at outdoor games. Most of tat, the Gentlewoman says, they like what they call her "joyful religion." To tell the truth, The Swedes have suffered a little from the C4vin- istic views held by their Queen and Crown Prin- cess, and the accepted fact that Princess Margaret does not believe in a Sabbath spent in gloom comes in the nature of a relief to her , future subjects.

SMART COUNTRY COSTUME. In the sketch is shewn a smart little costume, •suitable for golf or country pursuits. It is carried out in a soft woollen material, in black-and-white ' shepherd's plaid. The skirt clears the ground all round, and is arranged in pleats stitched down to below the knees. The coat is finished with a short basque behind, and the fronts are cut short like an Eton -coat, while over the shoulders there are stitched straps. The collar and revers are

faced with scarlet cloth, and the belt is of the same coloured leather, fastening with a tilt buckle. The fronts of the coat are ornamented with plain gilt buttons. The sleeves, which are of the useful bishop shape, allow plenty of free- dom. and are easily put on over the blouse. They are drawn into cuffs faced with the scarlet cloth. The shirt blouse worn with this costume is of white flannel, finished at the neck with a red-and- white spotted tie.

div.head: CRICKET FOR GIRLS.
div.p: CRICKET FOR GIRLS.

At the conclusion of a cricket match at sew, the other evening, played in accordance with the terms of the will of the late Mr. Pring, a keen cricketer, who died in 1881, and who founded a fund to be devoted to the encouragement of cricket among the boys of the Royal village, an interesting announcement was made by Mr. Walter Tyler, the president of the movement. The committee had under consideration, he said, the question of encouraging cricket among the girls of the village, and as the result of their deliberations it was more than probable that next year a match similar to that now played by the boys would be held for girls ranging in age from eleven to fourteen years. A fund would probably be started among the residents, out of which prizes would be given to the girls who dis- tinguished themselves most in the Various de- partments of the game.

div.head: ULCERS FOR THIRTY YEARS. – – A Woman's Chronic Bad Leg Healed –
div.p: ULCERS FOR THIRTY YEARS. - - A Woman's Chronic Bad Leg Healed -
by Zam-Buk.

Next evening the foot pained me, and [found a small scab had formed on the braise. I applied ointments, but the scab spread, and running wounds appeared all over my leg up to the knee and down to the very toe ends. Nothing proved equal to checking the disease, which finally developed into several chronic ulcers. I tried everything that anyone told me of, but without avail. The pain was so bad i that I could not rest anywhere. At the Horncastle ; Dispensary they treated my disease carefully, but in ' vain. My leg became worse. I was unable to walk even about the house without support,and the pain was some- thing terrible. At times the ulcers would get a little healthier,but the scabs always came away,to reveal as had wounds as ever. A neighbour thought I should certainly ; lose my leg. Sometimes I lost the use of it altogether and once or twice I have fallen downstairs with it. For the last eighteen months of my martyrdom I never went outside the park gates, and they are only some two hundred yards away. At last my sister brought me a box of Zam-Buk. div.head: REVISING THE LISTS.
div.p: REVISING THE LISTS.
The Barrister Compliments the Warrington Political Agents.

The work of revising the,voter's lists was continued at the Town Hall on Friday evening and Saturday morning by Mr. James T. Foard.revising barrister,and completed on Monday morning. There was very little business of public interest. Mr. J. Howes, jun., represented the Liberal party, and Mr. W. Holbrook and Mr. Herbert Hayes appeared on behalf of the Conservatives. Messrs. A. T. Holloway (deputy town clerk), VV. H. Woodcock (assistant overseer) E. C. Cooper (assistant overseer for Winwick), T. G. Garnett and F. H. Aukland (reliev- ing officers) were:also present.

div.head: COUNCILLOR'S VOTE OBJECTED TO.
div.p: COUNCILLOR'S VOTE OBJECTED TO.

The Conservatives had lodged an objection to the vote of Councillor Peter Peacock who appeared before the barrister, and, in answer to Mr. Holbrook, said he lived at 135,Bewsey-road. Mr. Holbrook: You still occupy the house as a residence? Councillor Peacock : Yes.

Mr. Holbrook: My objection must fail in that case. I objected because I thought he resided beyond the specified distance. He tells me that he only lived out of town for a few months in summer. The vote was allowed. A HARD CASE.

The Conservatives objected to the vote of Frederiok John Bennett, ironworker, of 100, Pierpoint-street, on the ground that he had received parish relief. on reference to Mr. Garnett's books it was found that the relief was given four days prior to the qualifying period and Bennett was therefore entitled to his vote which the barrister allowed.
Mr. Howes drew his Honour's special attention to the case, with a view to obtaining costs for Bennett, remarking that the objection was an extremely frivolous e.
Mr. Holbrook: The Clerk to the Guardians gave me a list of persona receiving relief and this name was included.

His Honour: You cannot say that this is a frivolous objection. It is not sustained and if it had come in the morning I might possibly have allowed costs. It is a case of hardship,but the world is made up of hardships. Mr. Bowes said Bennett worked at one of the forges and had lost a " heat" in order to attend the Court on Friday evening. The Barrister : I never give costs at an evening sitting. I should not have considered the objection frivolous even in the morning. VOTE OF THANKS.

COMPLIMENT TO THE POLITICAL AGENTS. At the close of the proceedings on Monday, Mr. Holbrook said he wished to tender to his Honour hearty thanks for the manner in which he had received the cases brought before him. It had been a pleasure to go through the work, and the Court had passed off without a hitch. He also begged to congratulate the overseers, assistant overseer and staff on their good management of the list.

Mr. Howes seconded and said it was always a pleasure to come to the Warrington Revision Court because they seemed to be such a happy family. He would like to call attention to the fact that Mr. Hallaway, the newly-appointed deputy Town Clerk, had assisted the Court for the first time and he (Mr.Howes) was sure the impression Mr. Hallaway had given them was extremely agreeable. . . . .

In acknowledging the compliment, the Revising Barrister said he had occasion to remark last year that it appeared to him that the Warrington lists were as carefully prepared as it seemed humanly possible for them to be. He thought then the standard was one of the highest he had ever known of excellence and care with which the whole of the work had been carried through,and he was quite of that opinion still. He could not conceive how a list of such magnitude and con- taining so many names could be more carefully and exactly prepared, with fewer blunders, and from which the Revising Barrister could receive more assistance than he had received. With reference to the remark about their being a happy family, it had always seemed to him that it was a desirable thing if possible that, efficiency being the end and purpose of the revision,the one object to be pursued with a view to that efficiency was thetas little trouble should be given either to the reviser or—what was of much more importance— to the public as was possible, and that they should not be troubled with frivolous claims or annoyance. He could conscientiously say that the agents at that Court had done their work with prompti- tude and fidelity in the interests of the public. They had avoided all kinds of friction, the happy family in that sense being that they had striven strenuously, not with temper or acrimony, but with a judicious view to the efficiency of the task they vere undertaking, and to its perfection when it was accomplished.

div.p: SCIENCE NOTES GLEANINGS.

THE power going to waste at the Victoria Fars on the Zambesi River, in South Africa, is calc.:- lated at 25,000,000 horsepower, or five time th,t of Niagara. There is no doubting the future in store for the country in the immediate enviii..- ment of the Victoria Falls.

A STANDARD SCREW. • So important is the matter of a standard screw for gun-fittings and other accurate work that a committee of the War Office has spent four years upon the problem. A special lathe—the only one of its kind in the world—has been con- structed, and the screw at last produced is re- garded as a marvel of scientific accuracy. It is three feet long, with no deviation in any part of more than one 10,000 th part of an inch.

div.head: SYNTHETICAL PRODUCTION OF CAMPHOR.
div.p: SYNTHETICAL PRODUCTION OF CAMPHOR.

The high price of natural camphor has led to the investigation of processes by which this im- portant drug may be produced by partlal synthesis from cheaper materials. Turpentine is the usual starting point, and, according to two recent patents, It is first converted into its hydrochloride and thence either • into bornyl formate or bornyl acetate, the latter transforma- tion being effected, by heating at 130 deg. to 180 deg. C. with glacial acetic acid and anhydrous lead acetate. When decomposed by the usual processes of saponification, the formate and acetate yield borneol together with formic and acetic Acids respectively. , On oxidation, the borneol thus obtained is readily converted into camphor.

div.head: FASCINATING PROBLEMS IN GEOLOGY.
div.p: FASCINATING PROBLEMS IN GEOLOGY.

There can be no doubt, nays Science Siftings, that the character of the earth's interior and the physical laws which there prevail constitute the most fundamental object of geological and geo- physical research, while the results of successful investigation would be immediately applicable at least to the moon and Mars. No one questions that enormous pressures and very high tempera- tures exist near the earth's centre, while the quality of matter which constitutes the interior cannot be satisfactorily determined until we know how substances would behave , under extreme pressure and at temperatures approaching 2,ooodeg.C. There is every reason to suppose that under purely cubical compression dense, un- deformed solids are perfectly. elastic. Hence the basal problem of geophysics la to find the law of elastic compressibility. This cannot be accom- plished by direct means, but the task is, never- theless, not a hopeless one, and has been taken in hand.

div.head: ORIGIN OF COSMIC DUST.
div.p: ORIGIN OF COSMIC DUST.

The cosmic dust of the atmosphere is usually held to be of meteoric origin. The smaller meteorites, heated in their passage through the air, are dissipated into vapour, which remains suspended in the atmosphere as dust. Professor `Schaeberle contends, however, that part of this dust is of solar origin. And it has been sug- gested that magnetic storms and aurorte are ' caused by the earth passing through denser portions of streams of finely-divided matter thrown out by the sun. One of the greatest objections to this view is that no regularity in the ejections has been found in connection with tlrrestrial disturbances. Professor Schae- bode, however, contends that this irregularity is really in favour of the hypothesis. For, he points ouit, the force with which the particles are thrown out from the sun must be very vari- able. And a very, small change in the initial • velocity of ejection would make a large differ- ence in the time taken to reach the earth. Hence the irregularity of such phenomena favours the view that this may be due to streams of finely-divided matter of solar origin.

div.head: PARASITIC HABIT IN BIRDS:
div.p: PARASITIC HABIT IN BIRDS:

An observation by Mr. Edmund Selous on the nesting of the starling and woodpecker will probably be welcomed by evolutionists, as throwing light on the strange habits of the cuckoo.' This naturalist notes that when a wood- pecker's nesting hole has been usurped by a starling, the former will occasionally lay an egg in the nest. In this way, the woodpecker's egg may be hatched, and its young reared by the starling. And Mr. Selous suggests that in a similar way the parasitic habit of the cuckoo may have originated. Those birds which suc- ceeded in getting some Of .their eggs hatched in this manner would be supposed to obtain an ad- vantage in he struggle for life, and so, on the principle 'of natural selection, the habit would be developed. Considering the very obvious ad- vantage of getting its young reared for nothing, and the frequency with, which incidents such as the above must have occurred in the bird world, it is remarkable that the ctickoo is the only parasite among native birds.

div.head: CURES FOR DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: CURES FOR DRUNKENNESS.

In an article on Drug Treatment for In- ebriety," the British Medical Journal has had much to say against the extensively-advertised alleged cures. As is pointed out, chronic alcohol- ism produces lesions in most of the organs of the body, especially in the digestive and nervous systems, and any treatment, while it must be mainly directed to preventing the patient from continuing to poison himself with alcohol, must also have regard to means for restoring the func- tions of the damaged organs. Among drugs pos- sessing more or less specific action in alcoholism are ,hyossyamus, stramonium, and strychnine. Dr. Mcßride has also achieved the most satisfac- tory results with strychnine nitrate and atropine given hypodermically, while at the same time fluid extract of red cinchona bark was given by the mouth.

Dr. Blackwell Fenn has adopted treatment with hypodermic injections of strychnine sul- phate and of daturine or atropine; he gives at the same time a bitter tonic containing the chlorides of gold, sodium, and ammonium. Strychnine to some extent may be regarded as an antagonist of alcohol, since it restores the re- flex irritability when it is reduced by alcohol. Another authority attaches much importance to an anti-serum which produces in the horse a tolerance to alcohol. The injection of this serum, it is stated, causes the drunkard to lose the taste for spirits. , Ammonium chloride is also recommended by Dr. Fenn, and used in some of the advertised treatments.

A NEW INTERRUPTER. • In the Scientific American, Mr. Huck Gems. back describes an interrupter for currents not exceeding four to six volts, on what he believes to be a new principle. This instrument when • made according to the directions given will not consume more than Ito ampere, and will run , as long as may be, desired. A U-shaped baro- metric glass tube, about 15 centimetres in length, with a clear opening of about 3 millimetres is heated in an oxy-hydrogen flame, and drawn ° out at the base of the 13 so as to leave a capillary I bore not exceeding millimetre in diameter. 11 The tube is then partly filled with chemically ; pure mercury, and by drawing the air out of one limb of the U, the mercury is caused to pass through the capillary and to rise into the other limb, so as to stand at an equal height in each. I The apparatus is placed in a vessel of water, and two thin platinum wires, connected with the battery, are passed into the mercury in either limb, so that a feeble current may be transmitted through the U tube. In the middle of the capil- • liary there at on appears a bright bluish-green . spark, accompanied by a sharply pitched note, indicating interruptions of high frequency. The explanation as given is that the instant the cur- rent is closed the mercury at the smallest cross- section of the capillary tube will become in- tensely heated and will begin to boil, and the . force of the ebullition will cause momentary • rupture in the column of quicksilver. This will be °accompanied by a slight shocl4:, and the ex- ' panding metal will rise in the limbs of the U. Of course a vacuum will be created at tho point of rupture, and, as the tube is immersed in water, the mercury will cease boiling and will • immediately become cool and contract. In consequence of the atmospheric pressure. com- bined with the weight of mercury in the limb of the U. the metal is almost instantly again brought into contact to be at once heated and driven apart its before in a ceaseless cycle as long as the current is n•yi•itained. ,

div.head: GOLD IN/62A WATER.
div.p: GOLD IN/62A WATER.

The following process for extracting gold from sea wate're has recently been described in a Belgian patent. A ton of sea water is treated with about five Cubic. centimetres of concentrated aqueous stannous chloride, when the gold is converted into/ purple of Cassius and precipi- tated, together with magnesinin hydrate and the excess of tin, by the subsequent addition of about a pound of slaked lime. From this precipitate the gold is extracted with dilute potassium cyanide solution and isolated by any of the methods commonly used in the cyanide process (e.g., precipitation with zinc). Sea water from the mediterranean and the English Channel yielded 00 gold by this process, where- pi samples from the Atlantic furnished traces. For cooling a hot bearing, Professor Lecoecti suggests dissolving the usual oil in petroleum spirit, the evaporation of which will effect the !Doling desired.

div.head: PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
div.p: PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
Cases again heard at Warrington.

Warrington's passive resisters to the number of seven, were on Tuesday called before the magistrates to show cause why they should not pay the balance of the poor rate which was owing by them the sum in each instance being the amount allocated for the purpose of administerating the Education Act. The magistrates who were on the bench were Dr. Fox (presiding)Jand I Messrs. Irk. YOung and C. Jackson Holmes. The names of the persons summoned together with the amount of I the rate in dispute were :—William Clatworthy, 21, Lovely lane (Bs.) • Rev. W. J. Roberts, 30,Parker street, (68. 9d) ; Miss E. 'J. Fieldhouse. Bridge street, (12s. 9d); Edward Howard, 162 Padgate-lane (65.); Rev. C. L. Stowe, 4, Lodge-lane (Bs.) ; Thomas Dale, 76, Priestley- street (Is. Gd.) ; and Evan E. Hughes, 10, Crosfleld- street, (95.) I Mr. Clatworthy was first called upon to answer his summons. It did not require, he thought, that much need be said as they were well-known. Their purpose in coming there was a national and not a local one. They were continually protesting against the Educa- tion Act because they believed it to be unjust and until it was altered they would appear there. In appearing they presumed they would receive that courtesy which i had n the past been extended to them in the carrying out of those proceedings. The Rev. W. J. Roberts said he was not certain that the summons was legal. ' Mr. G. F. F. White (magistrates' clerk) : The summons is all right. Dr. Fox: You admit the rata is a legal one? Mr. Roberts : Yes. Dr. Fox: Then we have no alternative but to make the order. Mr. Roberts: I want you to take the summons into 'consideration. I Mr. White: There is nothing wrong with the
summons. Mr. Roberts : There is. The Chief Constablo : Yon must accept the Clerk's ruling. Mr. Roberts: That is unfair. This is supposed to be a court of justice and I am allowed to defend myself.

approve or me as a son-in-law.- ' My dear boy," said the duke, lying nobly fnr fear of giving offence. "there is no one the duchess and I would prefer: but surely it is a matter mainly between Sabina and your- self We cannot force her inclinations in such a matter."
The car shot across a narrow bridge to the left into Avenue Road.

"Of course not, sir," admitted the younger man, "but I thought that a word or a hint from you to her that I should be acceptable might go a long way." "So far I can help you, my dear fellow," said the duke, seeing a way, out of it without straining relations, "and sn far I will help you. I will see Sabina and tell her that her mother and I will be delighted to welcome you if she accepts you. But, of course, we cannot say or do more." "Thank you, sir, thank you," said Brank- sea._ "Of course, I .know that is all I can ask."
They both relapsed into silence as the car began climbing Fitzjohn's Avenue, breasting the steep hill without the semblance of an I effort.

As they reached Hampstead Heath, their defAination, Branksea leant forward and ex- tinguished the lamps. Halfway across the Heath lay a large house standing back from the road in its own grounds and surrounded by high trees. _

-Hampstead House was One of the historic houses of the Heath, a grand old Elizabethan mansion which had in its day been the scene of many gaieties. tinder the existing regime, however, the duchess did not find it suffi- ciently central, and it was only opened oc- casionally for garden parties or a reception in the season.
It was enclosed by a high red wall, spiked profusely against intruders, which rendered the garden invisible from the outside. Thus, even upon a bank-holiday, privacy was assured.
At the gate, which stood a. little way back from the main road, Branksea stopped the car and gave a low v,histle.

"I could go on talking all night on m) bobby, my particular bent--every man is ax egoist," he said with a laugh ; "but I won't.' And he changed the subject abruptly 131 asking Ben Nevis about his experiencet abroad, and dinner concluded with the con' versation general.
When the men were left alone over their coffee, Ben Nevis endeavoured to take up th( thread of Sir Hugo's dissertation on detectiola and apply it practically.
"Are there," he asked, lighting a cigarette; "any data in the 'White Rose' murders from which deductions can he drawn ? "

" The trouble is that there are so many," answered Sir Hugo, "and they are so obvious as to be elusive. Besides, they almost frighten one, the deductions are so stupendous: and a detective's first duty is to avoid obviousi yet palpably .false deductions. I could prove to. you, if necessary,' he added with a laugh, growing less • serious and concluding the subject with a paradox, "that the prime mover in the Mornington murder was the King or the Queen or the Duchess of Hamp- stead herself. You can prove anything if you only care to; it is like the average detective story written backwards." In the box at the theatre Bina fell to the share .of Ben Nevis, whilst Sir Hugo looked after Lady Grizelle, and they found them- selves growing very intimate. They had a great deal in common, and Charlie' was an ever ready half-way house between them, giving them a pretext for growing confidential.

Lady -Grizelle walched -them ,with amusecb and by no means dissatisfied, eyes. She had taken a great fancy to the newly returned wan- derer, and an idea was beginning to develop in her mind. Bina certainly showed more interest in him than she had ever before noticed her show in anyone of the opposite sex, and he was certainly without being awkward or rough, different in many respects from the crystallised type of man about town. , Their conversation, - though carried on in s. low tone, was particularly animated, and their appreciation of the play in consequence suffered. But the attraction of a man and a women for each other is infinitely more absorb- ing to both than the finest display of histrionic art or the wittiest comedy. In pursuance of her new idea, Lady Grizelle accepted an invitation from Ben Nevis to supper at the Savoy: but Sir Hugo, pleading for a good night's rest, went straight home from the theatre. They were very merry at supper and all seemed very pleased with themselves. Lady Grizelle felt like a fairy godmother in the elaboration of her plan: for not only was she particularly fond of Bina, but !she was at, the same time not particularly fond of her sister-in-law and loved to thwart her plans. Thus a double feminine motive, combined with caprice, was simul- taneously served. "Come down and spend the week-end with me, Lord Ben Nevis," she said, as the hands of the clock began to hint at departure. "I never spend Sunday in town, if I can help it, and 33ina is coming, too." " I shall be delighted," responded Ben Nevis promptly, recklessly throwing all en- gagements to the winds.

The gate swung noiselessly open. The car darted through: and it was closed behind ,them. "Good evening, Anderson," " said the

' Branksea drove the cat up the drive and stopped it a few yards beyond the front door. They both jumped out, the duke as active as, and more eager than, his companion. • At the front door the whistle was re- peated, and the password was again given. Then they entered the house, let in by an old woman, the wife of the gate-keeper. In the dark hall she took 'their coats and they passed on to a' door on the right. This stood slightly ajar, and a light shone through the crack. Inside, the, room was brightly lighted by wrought iron clusters of electric light—the only anachronism in the old banqueting hall. However, introduced with taste, it did not appear a very glaring one. . The walls were panelled with black oak up to the ceiling, which was of the same material. The windows were heavily curtained with red, which prevented the least ray of light from penetrating, even into the garden. On the walls hung some of the family portraits of the • Hampsteads-dead and gone Belsizes, committed to canvas by Vandyck, Lely, Reynolds, and the great painters of their day, in keeping with the sombre ' aspect of the old hall. . "The next business," went on the duke, "I' have been wanting the opportunity of a talk with you, sir, for several days," he be- after various letters and reports had been read gnu rather 'diffidently. Gordon rose with his thin lips compressed, nor was he a particular favourite of his: and, looking pale, but cool. moreover, he had an idea of what was coming. "Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen," he "I proposed to Lady Sabina two or three began, resting his knuckles on the' table, "I nights ago," went on Branksea slowly, "and am here to inform you that the order of the she refused me, as she has done so man other people.' I.` Then meet us at Waterloo at za on Saturday," said Lady Grizelle rising, "and escort us down. It is so nice to have someone to look after the luggage, and footmen are so careless."
On his way home Lord Ben Nevis actu- ally forgot the demands of propriety so far as to whistle out loud in the street.
CHAPTER XII.

neatn, 1 had no chance of getting near nim. They, by bad luck, kept immediately between him and me, until near Pond Street he picked up a hansom and got into it. At a signal my own man, one of the League, drove up, and I followed his cab, my heart in my mouth lest he should get away, as I thought of the awful risk we all ran and the death blow to the cause. He drove to the Carlton Club, where he stayed a few minutes, and' then by good luck he chose to walk home. The rest you will have read for yourselves in the daily papers, ladies and gentlemen. All I have to do is to announce formally that the order of the committee was successfully carried out." A slight shiver ran through one or two of the more timid conspirators. Lord Islington rose.

"Whilst congratulating the Earl of Annan- dale." he began, "upon the successful com- pletion of his mission, it must be evident to us all that a fearful risk was run. For the future I propose that, should the, good of the cause and the security of the committee make it necessary, owing .to some ill-judged refusal, to adopt a similar course, the member to whom the lot has fallen to execute the order should tide with the new-corner and join in his pro- test against so-called disloyalty. In this way lie could leave the house in his company and drive him away: and then no danger would be run again of an escape." . . .

"An admirable idea," said the duke, brush- ing the hair back off his forehead with his left hand, "and a very necessary one. It corn- meads itself to me as a wise course to adopt. Our next business is to draw lots in case of Lord Oddingly's refusal: and whoever draws the lot must bear this in mind."

While the simple arrangements were being got„ready, Mr. William Brinckley rose, look- ing very pale. "It seems to nip" he said, speaking nervously, 'that we are fast developing, into a murder club. I protest against it." The duke jumped up angrily, his eyes flashing.

" This, sir, is a revolution, not a massacre. We have begun, And now we cannot afford to stick at anything. Before joining us you should have counted the cost. If we had at first realised what it, would entail, we might all have entered upon this scheme for a right- ing a wrong of many years' standing a little less lightly: but now we must go on to the end, %dial ever it may be—to the very end. I fear it may involve more bloodshed than we thought. Perhaps," the Duke spoke very solemnly, "perhaps our own lives, already forfeit to the law, will have to be laid down in this -cause. We counted upon a bloodless revolution, but our calculations have proved all wrong. However, we have gone so far that we must go on. Let us, therefore, do so without flinching or blanching. It is too late for any one of us, man or woman, to draw back in the slightest." This outburst cowed the protesting member: and he relapsed into silence as a murmur of approval ran round the table. A silver urn was brought from the side- board and placed on the table in front of the duke, who carefully threw into it a cardboard ticket for every man present, counting them scrupulously. • On one was a black cross, heavy and unmis- takable. A breathless silence reigned through- out the room, and each man tried to appear unconcerned. But there was a strange tension on every side, and the women leant forward, all their brutal instincts aroused by the excitement of the moment and their finer feelings forgotten. Such a sensation was not to .be had every day in London ! _ .
"In order of age:" said the duke, in a sharp voice which sounded strange in the silence. "The youngest first." Branksea stepped forwa rd and drew a ticket.
He examined both sides. It was a blank.
An involuntary sound came from the lips of Lady Swanage. The Master of Gareloch followed. He, too, drew a blank.

Nothing could be heard in the room but the sound of heavy breathing. Every eye was turned upon Ellis Gordon, as he - stepped forward. Another blank, and Carruthers followed, smiling imperturbably. "A blank," he said, holding it up to the company, and he resumed his seat, still smiling. Lord Portcullis followed.
An exclamation, half hysterical, came from Mrs. Mclver. She had been the first to see the fatal cross.
Portcullis's usually ruddy face grew white for an instant, but he gave no other sign of feeling.

He-handed the duke the ticket. "At your orders, ladies and gentlemen," he said, bowing to the table. The duke took the small square of card- board, his eyes glistening with excitement. "We are safe in your hands, Lord Port- cullis," he said, motioning to Gprdon to re- move the urn and handing the othe a long, narrow case.
A scarcely audible murmur of relief broke from the lips of one or two of the less self- contained conspirators. .. . . • - • -

Slipping the- leather case into his breast pocket, Portcullis walked across to the side- board and poured himself out half a tumbler of brandy, which he drank off. Then he resumed his seat without a sign of feeling. So quickly and so quietly had everything been done that it was almost impossible to believe that a human life had been summarily disposed of, should circumstances demand. The duke broke the silence, which was growing oppressive._ _ _
"Has any member of the committee any name to suggest as an addition to our num- ber ? " he asked, looking round.
(To b: continued.)

"When my little boy was three months old his head broke out with a rash, which was very itchy and ran considerable watery fluid. We tried everything we could, but he got worse all the time till it spread to his arms, legs, and then to his entire body, and he came near dying. It itched so he would scratch till the blood ran, and a thin yellowish stuff would be all over his pillow in the morning. I had to put mittens on his hands to keep him from tearing his skin. He got so weak he took fainting spells and we would think him dying. He was almost a skel- eton and his little hands were thin like claws.

div.head: GOOD PROFIT FROM GRASS LAND.
div.p: GOOD PROFIT FROM GRASS LAND.

The hay crop on Mr. Ernest Parke's experimental grass fields at Kineton once again affords to occupiers of naturally poor clay land pasture a useful lesson on the results that may be achieved by a little enterprise in the direction of manuring. Both fields have been under grass about 13 years, and are annually mown in the summer and grazed in the autumn. The portions under experiment are divided into various half-acre plots, manured (in accordance with Dr. Dyers advice) with superphosphate, potash salts, and nitrate of soda separately and in combination; basic slag being sub- stituted for superphosphate in ?nepf the fields, the soil of which is poorer In lime than the other. In each case a plot is preserved for compari- son, which gets no manure except that incident- ally supplied by autumn grazing. The unmanured plot in Upper Hale Field this year gave 14 cwt. of hay per acre, which is more than the unmanured laud has yielded in any of the last three seasons. Basic slag alone (5 cwt. per acre) raised the yield to 2 tons of hay per acre, and nitrate of soda alone (2 cwt. per acre) to 2 tons 1 cwt. When both dressings were combined, the yield was 2 tons 5 cwt. of hay per acre—an increase of more than 11 ton of hay per acre over the yield of the unmanured land. The application of sulphate of potash in this field increased the yield only very slightly. On the field known as Five and Three Acres the unmanured plot this year gave 111 cwt. of hay per acre. The application of 3 cwt. of superphosphate per acre raised the crop to 1 ton, 16 cwt., and 2 cwt. per i acre of nitrate of soda alone raised t to 2 tons 1 cwt. Superphosphate and nitrate of soda used together gave 2 tons 3 cwt., which in this field was further increased to 2 tons 7 cwt. by the addition of 1 cwt. per acre of sulphate of potash, showing an increase of 12ton of hay per acre over the unmanured land, Durng the last four seasons the annual gain due to manuring on the best plots of the two fields has averaged nearly 12 ton of bay per acre, in return for an average annual expenditure of about £1 165. per acre for manures. Although the plots are all auturnn-grazed, and therefore under natural farming conditions, the manuring is already found, as at Rothamsted, to be altering the character of the herbage. The plots with nitrate alone are more grassy, and those with mineral manure alone have more clovers. The most flourishing mixture of herbage, however, as well as the heaviest crop, is found, as should be expected, on the plots receiving both nitro- genous and mineral manure.

The Prime Ministers MR. BALFOUR AND THE speech at North VOLUNTEERS. Berwick, a place at which he usually distinguishes himself at golf rather than by speech- making, has been called an attack on our Volun- teer forces. But that is scarcely an accurate des- cription. Mr. BALFOUR did not attack the Volun- teers. On the contrary, he admitted that they are indispensable—under conditions, and that they might become admirable if they would reorganise themselves under conditions not specified. The truth is that when the Prime Minister is in one of his fine, balancing moods his speeches, like the Scotch- man's jokes, are understood " wi' deefficulty." Mr. BALFOUR is an intellectual contortionist. He ties himself up in knots, and then unwinds in a manner that is quite puzzling to the beholder. Not long before the present Volunteer force was being formed the late POET-LAUREATE said of LOUIS NAPOLEON, who was then our ally, with a freedom of speech that must have seemed shocking in days so long before KIPLING, that "only the devil knows what he means." That is unfortunately the case with the present head of his Majesty's Government.

From the North Barwick speech it is equally possible to conclude that Mr. BALFoun considers the Volunteers to be a vital part of the national equipment and that he believes them to be an expensive and useless burden. As to the expense, we may point out that it is by no moans phenomen- ally heavy. Of late days it has been decreasing from one Budget to another, until last year it was I brought down to less than a million and a quarter. This is as against nearly £30,000,000 paid for an Army which, according to Lord ROBERTS, is in no more fit condition to take the field than it was before the Boer War. One thing which Mr. BALrotat says without equivocation is that the Volunteer force has "now to justify its existence. It will not be permitted to be 'expensive without being useful.' How the force is to justify its existence otherwise than it has been doing for years past the Prime Minister does not state, nor does he toll us what he means by being useful. The Volunteers are designed for use in a particular emergency, and the degree 'to which tbey may be serviceable can only be determined when the emergency arises. Mr. BALFOUR'S point seems to be that as the Volunteer regiments were raised for the purpose of repelling invasion, and as, in his opinion—which, by the way, is not supported by Lord ROBERTS—no inva- sion on the great scale can take place, the Volun- teers should be made to justify themselves by becoming something which they are not —a second reserve, let us say, to the regular forces. If this is really what is in the Prime Minister's mind, it fully explains Mr. ARNOLD- FonsTßn's illegal circular. But the policy is one which, we unhesitatingly take it upou ourselves to declare, will meet with the approval neither of the Volunteers nor the nation.

Nebulous as he is in speeches like that delivered at North Berwick, there are nevertheless certain fixed ideas in Mr. B-4.LFOUR'S mind which nothing seems capable of dislodging. One of these is that India is constantly subject to invasion. This was the inspiration of the long House ot Commons speech in which he first unfolded his views about Oa impossibility of invading England. The Prime Minister has brought himself to believe that he is a great strategist. Lord ESHER has told him that he is!probably the greatest master of strategy since NeroLcoN. Thusencouraged, he proceeds with his strategy when the necessity for it has ceased to exist The invasion of India idea, which was once most caustically ridiculed by his predecessor in the Premiership, was at the base of his speech about the Volunteers. Never was such an invasion further outside the area of reasonable contempla- tion than it is at present; but neither the collapse of Russia as a fighting Power, nor the Anglo- Japanese Treaty, which has the defence of India for the subject of one of its main provisions, operites to rid Mr. BALFOUR of his wholly un- reasonable fears about our great Dependency,'and the explanation of his speech to the East Lothian Volanteers is really ta be found in his remarkable absorption by this ghost-like invasion of India theory. He reminds the Volunteers that they are parts of a groat system, " of one organic whale " ; he tells them that they are no longer useful for the purpose for which they were raised —that, in fact, they will never be called upon to repel anything but a small raid; then he proceeds to say that conscription for the defence of India is not to be thought of; and finally, that if our

Indian Army were engaged with an enemy on the North-West Frontier, and every strain were pot on the country to provide soldiers for that contest it was hard to see what could be done without the Volunteers. And there the whole secret is out. Mr. BALFOUR wiskes to convert the civilian regi- ments into a fighting force to be despatched to India to make up for the difficulty of recruiting troops for the regular Army. That, no doubt, is what he means by "becoming useful."

Th a Warrington THE MUSICAL SOCIETY. Musical Society has entered upon what is hoped will be a successful season, and on Mon- day evening the usual businesses of the annual meeting was transacted. There was a unanimity of opinion that the Society is excellently served by its officers and only one change of any moment —and that compulsory—was snade. Alter fifteen years' devoted service. Mr. W. E. Atkin resigned the hon. secretaryship and the mem- bers were unanimous in according him a well-deserved vote of thanks. He has always zealously guarded the interests of the Society and it is a matter for regret that he is obliged to relinquish the reins of office. In Mr. Cyril Gough he will have a worthy successor who by his enthusiastic and capable efforts in the cperatic performances has shown his keen desire to assist the Society's work. The chairman(Mr. F. Monks) hinted that the society would be able to obtain grant from the Education Committee for the teaching of elementary instrumental music. TOis opens up an interesting subject but until a more definite proposal is placed before the town it would be somewhat premature to pronounce an opinion oil it.

The tragically THE FATALITY OF GOLF. siidden death of Mr. R. G. Henshall on Tuesday at the Appleton Golf Links and aa almost identical happening at Skegness Golf Links on the same evening suggest that there is a fatality about golf hitherto unsuspected. Not by any stretch of imagination could golf be termed dangerous game, though the flying ball has been known to inflict grave injury, but it apparently has its perils for the middle-aged man who leads a sedentary life. Both gentlemen we refer to died from an apoplectic seisure presumably brought on by the exertion necessary to the game, and their sad end must exercise a disturbing influence on fellow-golfers who have passed the meridian of life. Probably, however, the majority mal safely neglect what seems to be a warning not to play golf. The ryal and ancient game with its health-giving concomitants, •- • most certainly prolongs more lives than it / shortens. The late Mr. Henshall was a man who thoroughly enjoyed his golf, and he was wont to say that it hal added ten years to his life. • . Obviously the deceased gentleman felt very much' better in health as a result of the exercise he 7 obtained at Appleton, and we can only conclude. with a certain amount of fatalism that in the , Divine order of things Mr. Henshall's life had run its course. As a man he was very greatly res- pected and esteemed in the community which had witnessed his life's labours, and his sudden end „ evokes widespread sorrow, and deep syropattlY with the bereaved family. •.

The position of matters re THE WATERWORKS lating to Mr. LK COO CONTRACT, tract with the Water Cora- mittee has altered considerably since our last issue. At the meeting of the Genera Purposes Committee on Friday night last an in' vestigkition into the documents relating to they contract was agreed upon and a strong committee. appointed. This committee of inquiry,the fourth' of its kind in Warrington, has already met and recommended the employment of en expert civil engineer to go into the contract and a short— hand writer to record the proceedings. TheEe.;l, recommendations, together with the confirmation 7; of the appointment of the Comrnitttee, will be the subject matter of a special Council meeting on Monday evening next. During the discussion at last Friday night's meeting the Mayor and DapiltY Mayor appeared sceptical of any genuine public desire that "the air should be cleared, but after the large meeting of ratepayers in Parr Hall last (Thursday) night and the unanimous feeling evinced in favour of a thorough investigation there should now be no doubt upon the point in the official mind. Why a contract let at £24,400 should swell into £57,000 and why even members of the responsible committee should be refused information relative thereto are questions that the public is determined shall be answered. The policy of secrecy, so recently condemned by Alderruan Pierpoint, has engendered suspicion,and the good name of the town will never be restored until that suspicion is removed and the fanlight of publicity heats upon the doings of the Toqe Council, its committees, and its members.

When TarnmatlY Hall was defeated in the fight for the , control of the administration of New York City ,• „ purity was supposed to have won a victory. Judging from what we have heard since, however, , it was only party after all that triumphed. This is what we should janee from the conteA which is being waged on the other side at the presenV time. Mr. William Travers Jerome has been Dis" trict-Attorney for four years. His time is up 01 January Ist next and he wants to be re-electee• Since he has held the office, however, Mr. Jerowe' has learnt that the man who owes his prefermee° to a party is not a free agent to do the puhlic'e work. He is not responsible to the public, but tct; the party. He has, therefore, made an appeal te' the people. He wants to be nominated for hie office, not by a party organisation, but by a public petition, so that if he is elected he will have that feeling of responsibility towards those whe elected him which the party-nominated office" holders cannot have. The issues that divide the . people in national political ailairs, says Mr. Jerome, ' have no real applications to the questions which arise in local affairs. That is a truth which inos of us recognise, though few even in England I...ieve the courage to throw off the party bonds. 31,r• Jerome's doctrine has been pretty well received _lO New York by the independent section of the Press' but it, remains to be seen whether the Par,9's organisations which are naturally opposed to Lui attitude will be strong enough to defeat his aims.

div.head: GRAPPEN HALL.
div.p: GRAPPEN HALL.

PARISH COUNCIL MEETING. On Tuesday evening a meeting was held in the schoolroom under the presidency of Mr. J. C. part. There were present :—Messrs. Kaye, Smith, Ellison, Warburton, Bradford, Jenkins and Woodcock (clerk). Mr. Woodcock read the statement of the oversee' which showed a still advancing state of the expenditure. —Mr. Jenkins said he had been asked to bring to the notice of the Council the very defective state of the drain opposite the old Rectory in the village. When- ever there was heavy rain the roadway for about twent9 yards was flooded to the depth of a foot at least. Tbi? had happened three times during the past month am. anyone having business on the other side had to trespael through Mr. Wild's garden, going in at the one gate and coming out at the other. Of course this kind of thing could not go on. Then there were many children attendin,, the school who lived on the other side of the canal, and to expect them to wade through this minia- ture lake and sit in their wet things for hours svas, asking too much however desirable theirpresence be for purposes connected with the registrar. et moved, that they write to the Runcorn Rural Distric Council, calling their attention to the defective ersl°2' and asking that the matter may receive prmaPb attention.—Mr. Kaye said he could support all 31r- Jenkins had said and would second the resolution; This was carried unanimously.—Mr. Jenkins then sal that after what was said at the last meeting he woh. simply submit the following resolution " that we wit° to the County Council asking them if the ditch in Or; Long's field opposite Mr. Dakin's house Knntsford-w4 had been piped and filled in at the expense of the Count; —No one seconded the resolution and Mr. Jerisl said he was neither suprised nor disappointed at dee being no seconder' but why the Council should hesitata or be af mid to ask at whose expense the work was sol3e he failed to understand.—Mr. Parr then moved thlt vote of condolence be sent from the Council teal° family of the late Rector who had laboured so taal years in the parish and who was so highly esteemed hi all. This was carried and the Clerk desired to write'
that effect..

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON. •
div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON. •
I
p
I

Everybody in Wales is not quite so cOnfident that Mr, It. A. Naylor will oust Mr. Lloyd-George from .Carnarvon Boroughs as the Unionist candidate himself is. Even Mr. Fincham, the Primrose Leaguer, („ doubts very much whether they can do it. The Liberals have no doubt on the matter at all. They , e quite sure Mr. Naylor can't do it. , It is probable that Mr. W. H. Lever, of Port Sun- light fame, will again stand as the Liberal candidate .for the Wirral Division at the next general election. 'On the last occasion on whichhe contested the division )fr. Lever reduced the Conservative majority by 1,543. lie is a powerful speaker, especially on the subject of ree Trade, and his many friends in Warrington and . district will wish him success in his big undertaking * * * Out of ten members of the Water Committee only _ .._ ... .

three-, inclusive of Councillor Pemberton, were present at the important meeting on Friday evening, when an Investigation Committee was appointed to go into Lawson's contract. Councillor Magi= remarked : " This is how the Water Committee has always been on this subject. If the Committee was doing its duty there would be someone to represent it." However the investigation turns out, the Committee will have considerable difficulty in rehabilitating itself in public Confidence. * * * With a record for the season of only four victories out of twenty-two matches our local cricket eleven has nothing to be proud of. There seems to be plenty. 'of young blood in the Club, but there is not that earnest i interest n the game which is essential to success. If we are rightly informed the mid-week practices have been very poorly attended, and this must be in some measure responsible for the poor show the Club has made in the new League. There will have tett be a general smartening up if public support for the club is to be assured. .

* * * Ih The" Heathens " are showing that they possess , nite an advanced notion of civilization, notwith- tanding the recent talk of rudimentary revenge on e Tramways Committee in the shape of a boycott. . he subject on the tapis just now is tree-planting and strong committee has been formed in order to tempt the beautification of the village by such eans. Such an excellent idea is worthy of all raise. There is sufficient newness about Stockton eath— as witness Dundonald Avenue and Kimberly rive— to make tree-planting a matter of no great ifficulty, and systematic effort should enhance the strict immensely.

* * * A letter we have received from the Rev. J. Stratton, Workingham, Berks. draws attention to the "Spurious IMorts ' in which many Britishers from time to time Indulge, such as hunting park-deer, rabbit-Coursing, and the shooting of birds from traps. Mr. Stratton 'calls for assistance in exposing any cruelties connected With these diversions, and urges the support of Mr. `Corrie-Grant's Spurious Sports Bill. In this connection we notice that on Tuesday the Quantock stag-hounds hunted a -stag right into the town of Minehead where it was killed in the street in the presence of hundreds of spectators. An edifying spectacle truly, and well- 'warranting the term " spurious sport." .„." Survival of the fittest " is an inexorable law. , , -tee thing which is fittest for any environment will Prevail and flourish in it. In an environment based upon getting all you can out of your neighbour and Riving as little as you can, the sharpest wits are the fittest, and those who succeed are the Colonel Norths, the Barney Barnatos, the Whitaker Wrights, the llockefellers, etc. In an environment based on brother- hood, the purest spirits will be the fittest, and those who succeed will be those who love their kind and do most. to make the world beautiful.—Henry Holiday in the " Daily News." * * * At the Trades Council meeting on Tuesday, when it Was agreed to support the candidature of Mr. E. Plinston for one of the wards next November, Mr. o Buckley said he " attributed their miserable failure to get the fair-wage clause of the Town Council into hip-shape order to the fact that there were not enough Labour representatives on that body." We have no I Objection to Mr. Plinston's candidature, but we do dessent from Mr. 0. Buckley. The fair-wage clause already secures the payment of a fair wage and a Jrtandar.i wage and is also "shipshape." What it does not specify is a Trale UAion wage, and it would be neither fair nor ship-shape if it did. * * * The Musical Society loses a very valuable officer by the resignation of Mr. W. E. Atkin from the secretary- 'shill, after about fifteen years "approved " service— to use a military expression. Very genuine and earnest expressions of regret were heard on all sides at, the annual meeting of the Society on Monday, for Mr. Atkin, by his strict attention to duty, by his aptitude and tact, has earned the esteem and goodwill of all the members. It ,is the general opinion that his successor Mr. Gough has a difficult task to fulfil, but that he gives every promise of succeeding. We are sure that, along with Mr. Atkin and the Society's members, the musical public in Warrington wish him well. * * * The Appleton Primrose Leaguers had a great field day on Saturday. There was tea-drinking, speech- Making, and a bun-biting contest. The latter is des- cribed as having been particularly amusing, but the aPeech by Mr. Fincham, provincial secretary to the Grand Council of the Habitation, appears to have run it pretty close in that respect. The speaker went to ,the trouble of assuring his audience that " he did not know a perfect woman, although he was married," took occasion to complain of Sir Henry Compbell- ttannerman's "double-barrelled name," dwelt upon Japan's glorious fighting, and wound up by beating the" patriotic " big drum. We look in vain for any attempt to deal with the fiscal question or other great toPica of the day. Can it be that even the faithful Primrose Leaguers are fighting shy of the" raging and tearing" propaganda? "Life is fall of hardships," was the only consolation Which the Revising Barrister could offer a working- ala„ n who appeared before him at Warrington on -t'riday evening and who was undoubtedly labouring ender a grievance. The Conservatives lodged an objection to his vote which they were unable to sus- lain, and consequently the man retained his right to exercise the franchise. But in order to attend the Court he had lost a turn at his work and quite natur- '3llY considered he was entitled to costs. The •arrister, however, declined to allow him anything on the ground that he never gave costs at an evening Sitting. Had the man appeared before him in the atorning he might have obtained some compensation. The case was a hard one and we venture to think that -even the rules of the Court might have been relaxed to meet it.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
Liverpool to Warrington on a Stolen Bicycle.

Florent Gielen, twenty-two years of age, a Belgian, stated to have been long resident in France, was charged at Dale street Police Court, Liverpool on Monday, with stealing a bicycle, value £3,the property of the Post-master General. The machine was stolen from outside the West Derby Post Office, Mill lane, on September 9th. The same evening the prisoner was seen riding a red enamelled bicycle at Warrington and was arrested. Through the interpreter he said in French. "I bought the bicycle from a man in Lime- street, Liverpool for 205." He was remanded till Friday. PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASRIRE.—AdVt. Alliance Box Company, Ltd. , .

At a general meeting of the shareholders of the above Company, held on September 3rd., at the Reltis- tered Offices, Alliance Works, Orford-lane, Warring- ton, Mr. A. C. Russell presid;ng, a satisfactory report of the Company's trading for the half year ending June 30th was received and adopted. The peliod covered by the balance sheet shows a substantial profit. It was resolved to pay a dividend on the preference and ordinary shares at the rate of 5 per cent, per annum, free of income tax, and to carry forward a balance of £l6l 12s. sd. to next half year's accounts. The reserve fund was maintained as at last balance, being nearly equal to 10 per cent of the Company's issued capital. Much gratification was expressed at the satisfactory progress which has been made since the inception of the business five years ago by Mr. F. Maginn, the present managing director. It was decided to still further extend the scope of the com- pany's business, and arrangements are now being made with that object in view. Mr. A. C. Russell I was unanimously re-elected chairman for the ensuing year, and Mr. W. H. Bolton who retired by rotation was again appointed a director. Mr. J. R. Williams, Chartered Accountant, 45, Sankey-street; was also re-elected the company's auditor.

div.head: tired feeling.—(Advt.) Ancient Order of Forresters, Warrington District.
div.p: tired feeling.—(Advt.) Ancient Order of Forresters, Warrington District.

• On Saturday the members of the above dlstrict held their annual trip, the place selected for the half-day being Belle Vue. About 400 members their wives and friends, left the Central Station promptly at 2.15 and after a nice rim arrived at Belle Vue Station at 3 o'clock, the weather was very unfavoifrable rain falling all the afternoon, but it did not damp the enthusiasm of the trippers in seeing the sights, visiting the gardens and the various houses containing the animals. Time passed very pleasantly. Tea was served at 5.30 and after the inner man was appeased a short meeting was held, Bro. W. Flipkiss, D.C.R., presiding. P.D.C.R., Bro. G. Maybury, in a short speech introduced to the brethren three members of the Manchester District. Bro. E. Farrow District Secretary of Manchester said he was very pleased to be present that afternoon to give a hearty welcome to their brethren from Warrington on their visit within the confines of the Manchester District, visits like these between members of the various districts tended to promote a larger spirit of brotherhood amongst the members of such a large order, and he trusted that the friendship and brotherhood existing between the two districts would continue for many years. Bro. G. Smith, Secretary:of the North-Western Federation also gave a hearty welcome, he was, he said, looking for- ward to the visit of the Federation to Warrington with great pleasure and he trusted that the meeting would be of advantage to the members of the Warring- ton District. Bro. Dolby, P.D.C.R. of Manchester, in a few remarks said he hoped that the result of that r trip to Belle Vue would be more new members for the Warrington District. The members than dispersed for the remainder of the evening, time passed very quickly and the return journey commenced at 10.15 Warrington being reached at 11 o'clock.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. R. G. HENSHALL.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. R. G. HENSHALL.
Tragic _ End on tha Golf Links.

A. profound sensation was created in Warrington on Tuesday evening when it became known that Mr. Robert George Henshall, the manager of the Warring- ton branch of the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Company, had died with painful suddenness. The deceased gentlemen was an enthusiastic member of the Warrington Golf: Club and at six o'clock was playing on the links at Appleton. He appeared to be in better form than usual and played a round with Dr. Nadel' and Mr. Thomas Cooper, solicitor. As Dr. Naden had to leave, Mr. Cooper ;and Mr. Henshall entered upon a second round of the course. Mr. Henshall was" bunkered," his opponent at that time being some distance in advance. Having played his ball out of the bunker Mr. Henshall was following it up when he suddenly fell to the ground. Mr. Cooper immediately went to his assistance and Messrs. James Richardson, Henry Greenall, Henry Roberts, W. E. Fowler and Major Holmes R.A.M.C.(of Orford Barracks)who were playing on the field were also quickly on the scene.Majcr Holmes saw that Mr. Henihall's condition was hopeless and I he expired in a few minutes. In the mean- time Dr. Parker was telephoned for but when he i arrived life was extinct. The deceased gentleman , was carried into the pavilion and later was ramoved to his home, Norwood, Latchford, in the Warrington! police horse] ambulance. Mr. Henshall, it appears I had had an apoplectic seizure and it was not ' deemed necessary to hold an inquest. The deceased gentleman was held in deep respect by a very large circle and the news of his tragic end came as a shock and was received with genuine regret. Earlier in the day he had discharged his duties at the bank and appeared to be in his usual good health and spirits. Mr. Henshall had led a busy and uselnl life. Born at Stya.l, Cheshire, in 1811 he entered the service of the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Co., Ltd., as a junior clerk at Warrington in 1864. He displayed great aptitude for the work and by conscientious service soon gained the confidence I of his employers, with the result that his promotion was rapid and in nine years he became cashier. Ten ' years later he was appointed accountant and in 1890 he was transferred to Haslingden (Lancashire) to take I control of tho bank there. In 1893 the management 1 of the Warrington hank became vacant by the death of I Mr. Wm. Barlow (who passed away very suddenly) and 1 Mr. Henshall was appointed to that very important I post. He fulfilled the duties with marked ability up I to the time of his death, and his kindly and genial ' disposition earned for him the esteem of all with whom he came into contact. He was prominently identified , with the Wesleyan Methodist Church, and for manyl years attended Bold-street Church, having filled all the offices as well as acting as delegate to the conferences and synods. He acted as treasurer for the Warrington Circuit to- the Foreign l'issionary Society, and did much to encourage support of that worthy object. Since the erection of the new church at Latchford Mr. Henshall had worshipped there, and had rendered valuable ser- vice in various important offices. He was society steward, treasurer to the trustees and secretary to the Foreign Missionary fund of the church. His loss will be very keenly felt and it will indeed be difficult to fill his place. The deepest sympathy is expressed with the widow and family (one son and three daughters) in their bereavement.

THE FUNERAL. The funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery this (Friday) afternoon amid many manifestations of regret. The cortege left the house at 12.30 and pro- ceeded to Bold-street Wesleyan Church, where a short service was conducted by the Revs. J. Manning and J. Gunnell, in the presence of A huge congregation. There was a representative gathering of local gentle- men at the graveside. The chief mourners were Mr. Harold G. Henshall (son), Mr. and Mrs. Frank Hick- man (son-in-law and daughter), Miss Mabel Henshall (daughter), Mr. Edward Gandy, Mrs. Waterwerth, Lewes (sister), Mrs. Witchel, South Wales (sister), Mrs. Walker. Rhyl (sister), Mr. Partin.ton, Knutsford, Mr.

—.),aix. Vartingtb. , Partington, Northwich, and Mr. Anderson, Nortliwich (hrothers-in-law). The Wesleyan body were repre- sented by the circuit stewards—Messrs. .1. a Withensbaw) and J. Lipson, and in addition the officers connected with the various churches in the circuit were in attendance. Amongst others present were Messrs. William Hickman, William Silcock (representing Parr's Bank), W. J. Forshaw, .Tohn Fairhurst (borough treasurer), C. Leigh (representing Messrs. T. and J. L. Tanstall and Co.), J. Billies (representing the Warrington Golf Club), J. Broadbent, Manchester (Superintendent of the Man- chester and Liverpool District Banking Company's branches), Grocott (representing the Warrington branch of the Bank, J. Dodds (representing the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd.), ,i W. H. Bleckly, J. J. Blackly, Grosvenor (representing the Union Bank of Manchester, Warrington Brinell), John Gandy, Edwin Richardson, Sankey, (Croft), Taylor (representing the Firth Mattress Co)., and representatives were•also present from Messrs. NV. I). Houghton and Co., Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., Ltd., and Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Haydock.

ANOTHER DEATH AFTER GOLFING. Mr. Thomas Bljr Minor, director and prornotor of mission vessels to the North Sea fisheries. died suddenly of apoplexy at Skegness on Tuesday evening soon after golfing on-the links.
CREAMY.
Mr. R. L. OUTHWAITE, WIIO WILL SPEAK IN PARR BALL NEXT TUESDAY EVENING ON CHINESE LABOUR.

who was sent out from that colony to investigate the Chinese labour system on the spot. He can claim to be one of the greatest living authorities on the subject, having studied it in all its bearings. His speech therefore should be full of interest as throwing fresh light upon a question which has been much dis- cussed in Warrington. Our readers will also be pleased to hear that Mr. F. Neilson, candidate for the Newport Division of Shropshire, has promised to address the meeting. On the occasion of his recent visit to Warrington he created a very favourable impression by his powerful addresses—not without their touches of humour—and there should be a large muster to listen to him again. Councillor James Evans will take the chair at 7.30.
