div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Lonsdale—Shann.

Miss.. Amy Vereua Shann, younger daughter of Sir I Thomas Thornhill Shaun (Lord Mayor of Manchester) land sister to the Lady Mayoress, was married yesterday at St. Paul's Church, Heaton Moor, to Mr. Herbert Lonsdale, youngest son of Mr. Charles Lonsiale, of Chester, and who for 30 years was connected with Messrs. Greenall's Distillery, leaving Warrington five ' years ago. The officiating clergy were the Rev. N. H. Smart and,. the Rev. R. Pratt. The ceremony created considerable stir in the Heaton Moor and Heaton Mersey districts, where the bride's family is of course so well known. The bride (who was given away by her father) wore a dress of ivory duchesse satin, with Brussels net veil and wreath of myrtle. The bride- groom's " best man " was Mr. Ernest Lonsdale, while the bridesmaids, four in number, were Miss Mabel Lons- dale, Miss Edith Sutcliffe, Miss Lillie Jones, and Miss Grace Howard. After the wedding ceremony there was a reception at Meadow Bank, Heaton Mersey, the resi- dence 01 Sir Thomas Shann. Amongst the guests were Sir James by and Lady Hoy, the Mayor of Salford (Sir William Stephens), Sir W. H. Bailey, .51r. Coun- cillor Rayle and Mrs. Hoyle, Mr. Alderman Rushworth, Mr. Councillor Dreyfus, Mr. and Mrs. Arthur A. Howarth, Mr. and Mrs. C. H. Scott, Dr. and Mrs. Meek, Mr. John Philips (Postmaster of Manchester) and Mr. William Sutcliffe.—Mr. and Mrs. Lonsdale will take up their residence at Stockton Heath.

div.head: Gandy—Bottomley.
div.p: Gandy—Bottomley.

An interesting local wedding was solemnized at the Parish Church on Thursday the contracting parties being Miss Florence Bottomley, daughter of Mr. George Bottomlay, Manchester-road, and Mr. John Henry. Gandy, second son of Mr. John Gandy, Buttermarket- street. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. G. A. Dearden in the presence of a large congregation. The bride who was given away by her father was attired in a dress of brown poplin trimmed with brown chiffon and cream embroidered chiffon. She also wore a brown chiffon hat trimmed with cream roses and ostrich feathers, and carried a shower bouquet of white lilies and asters. The bridesmaids, the Misses Lucy and Alice Bottotnley, wore dresses of pale blue nuns' veiling, trimmed with cream briar-stitching, and white hats, and carried bouquets of marguerites. The reception was held at the house of the bride's father, after which the happy couple left for Ethyl and North Wales. The bride travelled in a grey costume with hat to match. Many beautiful presents were received.

div.head: Willett—Cook.
div.p: Willett—Cook.

There was a pretty wedding at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Thursday, the contracting parties being Miss Ada Cook, daughter of Mr. Nathan Cook, The Poplars, Lovely-lane, and Mr. John William Willett, son of Mr. John Willett, Dalton Bank. The event aroused con- siderable local interest and the ceremony which was performed by the Rev. H. Wall, was witnessed by a large congregation. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a dress of cream silk trimmed with white chiffon, and a hat to match. She carried a shower ho, quet of white lilies. There were four bridesmaids. The Misses Cissy Willett, Clara Willett and Stringer were attired in dresses of biscuit-coloured crepe-de-chine with black picture hats, while Miss Annie Willett wore a dress of blue voile trimmed with Valenciennes lace and white'chiffon,with black picture hat. The bridesmaids carried bou4uets of lilies of the valley. Mr. R. W. Cook discharged the duties of best man. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., pre- sided at the organ ~nd played suitable selections. The reception was held at the Winmarleigh Cafe after which the happy couple left for Blackpool where the honey- moon is being spent. The bride travelled in a grey costume with hat to match. Numerous presents were received.

div.head: Waring—Macleod.
div.p: Waring—Macleod.

On Tuesday afternoon, September sth, the wedding took place at St. Cuthbert's Church, Bedford, of Miss Gita Macleod, the eldest daughter of Mr. Bannatyne I Macleod, barrister-at-law, of No. 18, Rothsay-road, and j grand-daughter of Colonel W. N. Wroughton and Mr. Henry Allen Waring, son of Captain I W. Waring, of Latchford House, Warrington. Mr.H.A. I Waring is Principal of the Vellore Police School, Madras, and as the bride is a former pupil of the Bed- ford High School the felicitous event was one of con- siderable interest to a wide circle of friends. The occasion was favoured with beautiful weather. The marriage service was conducted by the Rev. J. Lewis Hughes, assisted by the Rev. A. W. B. Higgens, late of Indian Civil Service. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a dress of white crepe de chine, trimmed with Brussels lace and orange blossom, with satin train hanging from the shoulders, and her orna- ments were opals. The bridemaids were Miss Dyott and Miss Waring (sister of the bridegroom), and Miss Clare i Macleod, who acted as flower girl, while Master Roland Macleod was the page. The bridesmaids wore dresses of mauve, and cream eolienne skirts, trimmed with ruchings of white ratio ribbon ; also white crino- line picture hats trimmed with shaded pansies, and long strings of pale mauve chiffon ; gold brooches, the ! gift of the bridegroom, and carried bouquets of mauve and white flov.ers. The bridegroom also presented a gold and ametheyst pin to the page. Captain Wilcocks, of the 78th Punjab infantry, acted as best man. The bride's mother wore a blue cloth costume, trimmed with lace and sable and white criaoline hat trimmed with white feathers, and carried a bouquet of crimson and white asters. The dress of the bridegroom's mother was of navy blue silk trimmed with cream lace, and her bouquet was composed of yellow cyrysanthemums. The service was partly choral Mr. Adams presided at the organ, and the hymns, " 0 perfect love" and " Lead us Heavenly Father," were sung. After the ceremony about sixty relatives and friends were entertained at the reception at 18, Roth- say-road. The cateting was provided by Miss Emerson Norman, who also supplied a handsome two-tier wedd- ing cake, ornamented with marguerites (the flower name of the bride), and white roses, the initials of the bride and bridegroom being represented on medallions. Miss Arnold made the dresses, and the flowers were supplied by Messrs. Laxton. The newly-united couple departed for \Vales, and will proceed to India at the end of October. The wedding presents were numerous and handsome.

div.head: VOLUNTEER SERGEANTS' PICNIC.
div.p: VOLUNTEER SERGEANTS' PICNIC.

The Sergeants of the Ist V.B. South Lancashire Regi- ment were most unfortunate in the choice of day for their annual picnic, which took place on Saturday last to Gateacre. Ile day opened bright, but fitful showers made the outlook anything but pro uising. A start was made at 1.50 p.m., about 50 sergeants taking advantage of the outing—which was extremely good considering that class firing at Altcar prevented the attendance of the stiff and a number of sergeants. On arrival at Gateacre the party, through Captain and Quarter- master A. 14% G. Potter, had the pleasure of going through Colonel Hall Walker's magnificent grounds—the head gardener acting as guide. Here again the weather intervened, the glass houses I being eagerly sought for. Nothing daunted .the Sergeants stuck the whole round and were delighted with the lovely collection of beautiful flowers which were shown. The kennels also were visited. After visiting the grounds the party left for the Elephant Hotel where arrangements had been made by the Mess President (Colour Sergeant J. Cliffe) to have their usual hot dinner. A bowling main which had been arranged had to be abandoned owing to the weather. A billiard handicap WaS immediately got up, but owing to the length of the journey however only the first round was played which resulted as follows : Col Sergt C. Russell ). 63 Col Srgt. T. Ashworth) 5G Band Mstr Richardson j Sergt Aikenhead. Col Sergt W. Woods 1,13 Sergt Woolstencroft. Sergt D. L. Owens. I" Sergt C. Dagnall. j2G Qt-Mstr Srgt Willcock 1. 63 Sergt G. Bebbington. 167 Col Sergt W. Spencer.) Mr. S. C. Gimson. The last was an extremely interesting game. The re - turn was made about 8.15 p.m. the party arriving in Warrington about 10.30. The transport arrangements were undertaken by Messrs. Magian Bros. and were I arried out in their usual first class style.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By " Ovalist."l

IThere was a vast difference between last Saturday's match with Oldham at Warrington and the previous one with Leigh, one being just as full as the other was devoid of interest. The Warrington men set about their work with a determination and dash which were in marked contrast to their lack-a-daisical methods against Leigh. The conclusion was unavoidable that the defeat of Leigh was accomplished without the team being extended in any way. Had the cup-holders played with the same vim as on Saturday then the Leighites must have suffered a severe handling. There is a vast difference between the calibre bf Leigh and Oldham and no one knows this better than the wearers of the primrose and blue. They could whack Leigh any time but they had to put in every ounce to get the better of Oldham, last season's champions.

j On last season's results Warrington and Oldham are of course the two crack clubs of the Union and the meeting between the Cup-holders and the League Champions was thus the tit-bit of the day. Friend " Philistine " came down in all his glory and assisted the local scribes to describe the .Homeric combat. Fortunately for the Warringtoniaus they gave a display which would have been creditable in any company. Oldham are not the team they once were in the days of Gwynn, APCutcheon, Varley and Jack Hurst, and they have now no men the equal of these lights of old, but they are still a powerful combination. While possessing no performer of outstanding brilliance, with the possible exception of that fine forward Joe Ferguson, they are well represented in all departments, and will, I imagine, play a big part in the season's campaign. As of old they are a-good drawing side, and the crowd at Warrington was very satisfactory considering the amount of rain that had fallen and was still hanging about. Luckily the Wilderspool turf is very absorbent, and the ground proved in good order.

A fine struggle for supremacy rewarded those who had braved the threatening elements. Right from the commencement the game was contested at a very fast pace, and probably not a man spared himseH one iota. The forward duel was really interesting, for both were powerful packs.and they struggled manfully for posses- sion of the ball. In the early stages of the game Oldham were the superior team and it looked as if the home citadel might fall at any moment. Tom Fletcher, the ex-international who assisted Oldham a few seasons back and has been out of football for some time since, proved that he was by no means a spent force. What with colliery accidents and the ravages of Father Time I had expected that the Seaton man would have detetiorated considerably, but he is still a centre worth having. It took the Warrington men all their time to prevent him breaking through the defence with his powerful play and but for the persistent way in which the home halves hung on to his legs at times he must have gone right through. If anybody can find ' me a pair of half-backs who can and will tackle better than Hockenhall and Brooks I want to be taken to them 'right away. They were extra superior on Saturday, and look like making as classy a pair as any in the League.

But for Fletcher's glimpses of greatness I think Warrington would have had a greater margiq than a penalty goal to nil. After the first ten minutes they settled down to a strong game and always seemed just a bit too good for the Oldham men. In the first half, Hockenhall twice made individual efforts worthy of his County form and from the second a try must have resulted but for Fletcher's great tackle. He took Isherwood sideways right on the line at full speed and squelched him in a fashion that none but a man with a two-stone advantage in weight could have equalled. As a consequence the Warrington man missed what was a certain try. At the time he was blamed for not passing to Fish, but I don't think selfishness can be urged against Isherwood, or even a lack of judgment on this occasion. He seemed bound to score and could hardly have anticipated Fletcher's fierce leap. In fact the Oldham man was not expected, and his sudden advent was decidedly ore trop. In addition to saving his side at this moment he nearly scalped young Kenyon a little later in trying a hurdle jump over his head. As a result Warrington were a man short for about one third of the game.

There was no score until well on in the second half when Fish landed a penalty goal for deliberate off side. Perhaps the Oldham men though they could spare this much, but they were in error. Though they did a fair amount of attacking later they were beaten off and could do no better than take desperate pot-shots at goal. No less than three of these were tried and once the red-hooped warriors rejoiced-- prematurely. Then the rain came down, not in single spots but in battalions. The panting forwards dripped and steamed, the backs tried to watch one another, and the ball slithered all ways but the intended direction of the kicker. The last quarter was there- fore somewhat inglorious, but the crowd saw it out and cheered a: hoarse-voiced and hearty cheer at the close when the wet but winning warriors of Warring- ton carried off tho spoils.

Praise all round is due to the victors, and it is difficult to discriminate. The half backs, as afore- said, were the heroes of the day, however, and were always a bit too good for Lees and White. Otherwise the teams were well matchedit Both full backs were smart and reliable and there is many a good kick left in the old war-horse" Dicky "Thomas.

Runcorn played their first match on Saturday and won it, the Hornets of Rochdale proving hardly equal to Houghton, Butterworth, Jolley and Co. These three are still the mainstays of the Runcorn team, and all distinguished themselves on Saturday. St Helens are still glorying in the accumulation of cheap points, and were very valorous at the expense of Morecambe Widnes, like their neighbours, did not open till last Saturday, but they made a less creditable debut. Hull Kingston Rovers were the visitors, and they just managed to win. Widnes were rather shorthanded, however, and missed several of their best players- Dai Davies' new team had to bow the knee to Halifax. but the ex-Warringtonian scored the only goal for his side.
Here is the League table with its points and per- centages. I have put Warrington at the top as they are the only team with a clean slate as the result of two matches :
The points are two for awn) and oae for a draw. The percentage ill calculated upon the basis of the total points possible.

There should be another fine contest at Wilderspoo to-day when 'Broughton Rangers make their appear- ance. So far the Rangers have had a chequered career. In their opening match they succumbed at home to Wigan in a most inglorious fashion by 23 points to 8 points. Last Saturday they went to Leigh and smote the Mather-lane crowd hip and thigh, fifteen points to nil being the total at the finish. Apparently the Rangers have pulled themselves together, and I have no doubt that they vrtll make a great effort to avenge themselves on Warrington for the crushing defeat near the end of last season. It will be renaem- / bared that with a weak team Warrington romped
round the Broughton men to the tune of 19 points to three points, after being pointless at half-time.

Fish and Shugars will be notable absentees from to-day's match, the vacancies being filled by Harris and Swift. Stmgars has a bad shoulder as the result of a knock received against Oldham. The team will ' be: Hallam, full back; Harris, Dickenson, Isherwood and Kenyon, threequarters ; Hockenhall and Brooks, half backs; Preston, Boardman, Thomas, Cook, Naylor, Jolley, Swift and Harmer, forwards.

Broughton Rangers will bring the following fifteen: —Poole, Hogg, Wilson (captain), Harry, Harris, Sam James, Will James, Trotter, Smith, Darleson, Preston, Ruddick, Winskill, Dram, Beetham, and Whitehead (selected from).

I made a slight error last week through not looking at my. fixture card. Instead of playing Oldham "A," Warrington" A" were away at Tyldesley in their opening Combination match. They gave a very good display against the old " Bongers and won by 2) punts to 5 points. By the way, I wonder how many Warrington supporters remember that Fish's first appearance at Warrington in a League match was a.gainst Tyldesley in the thys of " Buff " and W. Berry? The Lostock Gralam youth proved his worth at once by a remarkable run through the thick of the' Tyldesley men for a try under the posts.
The officials for to-days rnitcli are : Ttsferee, J. 13tickshavv, Stockport ; touch judges, W. H. Cowley, Runcorn, and E. Gordon, Widnes.

In Messrs. Dolan's window, Horsernarket-gtreet, ig to be seen the framed picture presented by Mr. W. R. Neil (President) to the Warrington Football Club in honour of the Northern Union Cup victory last April, The picture consists of elcellent portraits of the Cup team, the officials and committee of the duly, the cup and medals.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The committee of the Works Association were hoping that last Saturday they would be able to conclude the individual main but the weather willed otherwise, and on account of the rain the competition could not be resumed. It is hoped that the event will be more honoured to-day and that the Association will be enabled to conclude its season.

The draw for the championship competition for the prize of £5 given by Mr. E. England took place last (Thursday) evening. The entries have not come up to expectations and number about 30. It is, nevertheless, expected that some excellent trundling will on Satur- day be witnessed on the Corporation green in Victoria Park.

div.head: Cycling
div.p: Cycling

The cycling season which on the whale has been very successful is fast drawing to a close. Owing to the heavy rain the Warrington cycling club's run to Daven- ham, arranged for last Saturday, had to be cancelled. On Tuesday evening Stretton was the destination. The night was fine and the roads were in excellent order after the rain of the week-end, but there WAS only a. snAll turn-out. The run was made via Grappenhallitnd was thoroughly enjoyed. To-day's run is to Lower Peover, a favourite Cheshire resort. The concluding night run will be held on Tuesday to Sankey and will wind up with a " smoker "at the Chapel House.

div.head: following fitting lines in memory of the late Mr. D. Davies have been composed by an old member of the
div.p: The following fitting lines in memory of the late Mr. D. Davies have been composed by an old member of the
club :

. IN 11lEmortiAm. No more we'll listen to thy merry tales Of Cycle Tours in Counties far and near, Of week-end jaunts in Shropshire and in Wales, And moonlight spins thro' charming Delamer°. Familiar haunts wilt hear thy voice no more, The festive board will miss thy genial smile, The club runs too will not be as of yore, Without thy pleasantchat the journey to beguile.
Farewell, Dear "Pa," thy race'is run, The Line is crossed, the Judge has called thee home. W. 8., W.C.C.
D Darius, died July 26th, 1905. -- Angling.

The juvenile members of the Warrington Anglers' Association held a competition in the Bridowater Canal, at London Bridge, on Saturday. The arrangements for the event were excellent but the climatic conditions were of the worst possible character,rain falling heavily during the greater portion of the match. The fishing was superintended by Messrs. F. G. Emson and G.. Smith. There were 41 competitors and the prize winners were :—S. Minett. H. Jolley, T. Dixon, J. Pendleton, W. Larson. H. Well, T. Knight, and J. Shepherd. Arr unu3nal feature of the contest was that not a single roach was caught, all the limed weighed in being gudgeon.

On the 10th lust the members of the Royal Oak Branch Association visited Vale Royal where "13 corn- petitors took part in a match. Sport was excellent. The three first prize winners were S. Smith (lb. 6 oz.) E. Hart. and F. Summers. The prizes were distributed on Monday evening.

To-day the principal match of the season in connec- tion with the Warrington Association will be fished at Thelwall, when teams will fish for the shield. An excel- lent number of entries has been receiverland an exciting contest is promised. Any member of the Association not assisting a team can take part in the individual competition for the championship medal presented by Mr. J. Lyon Whittle and for prizes which total £lO.

An open contest will be fished at Mickle Trafford ore the 30th inst., and will consist of a roving match of three hours' duration. An open match will be fished at. Lymm on the 23rd inst., for which entries can be made on the bank up to three o'clock.

Some very fine specimens of course fish. particularly of roach and bream' have been taken at Rossett. The Bridgewater Canal has been rather unproductive of late and anglers generally have been disappointed. Rumour bath it, however, that a roach scaling 1;1bs. has been landed at Grappenhall. A trout about llb. in weight has been caught at Massey Brook. --- Cricket. The Warrington drib have just concluded their season and a disappointing one it has been. It had beca confi- dently hoped that the formation of the West Lancashire League would infuse new life into local cricket and Warrington were expected by their supporters to gain honours in the competition. Such poor displays have been given that the eleven only just avoided the woodea spoon, finishing last but one in the league. Altogether 2.2 matches were played, and of these only four were , won, whilst ten were lost and eight drawn. In the fixtures with Ashton-undor-Line and Werneth rain did not allow of any play at all. The victories were over Stanley, Prescot, St. Helens Recreation and Preston. Defeats were sustained at the hands of Newton (2), St. Helens (2), Wigan (2), St. Helens Recreation, Stanley, Earlestown and Bolton, whilst the undecided matches were played with Earlestown. Prescot, Bollington (2), Werneth, Preston, Bolton and Urmston.

The highest score of the season was made by 3fason, the popular professional, who compiled 2-13 against. Bolliogton. E. A. Connor, however' has displayed the most consistent good form and heads the batting averazes. Against Earlestown he scored 133 (not out) in brilliant style. Mason displayed the best bowling form, capturing 91 wickets.

Bawming the Thorn" at Appleton. The ancient and picturesque ceremony of "Ba,wming the thorn" was revived at Appleton Thorn on Thursday when a bazaar and fête in aid of the organ fund in connection with St. Cross Church were opened by Lady Brooke. The thorn tree which stands in the centre of the village was gaily bedecked with bunting and boys and girls walked round it hand in hand singing some quaint verses composed by the late Mr. R. E. Egerton-Warburton, of Arley MTh The chil- dren placed bunches of flowers on the rails surround- ing the tree and prizes were awarded for the best bouquets. Other attractions included old English. sports and motor rides, and a band was in attendance/.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
Annual Meeting.
MR W. E. ATKIN RESIGNS THE SECRETARYSHIP.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Musical Society was held in Cairo-street schools on Monday evening under the chairmanship of Mr. F. Monks a vice-president of the Society. There was a fair attend- ance, including the hon. secretary (Mr. W. E. Atkin). Mr. ATKIN expressed regret that the President (Mr. J. Charlton Parr) was not with them. In explanation, he might state that when he wrote to Mr. Parr in August asking him to preside as he had very kindly done more than once, Mr. Parr replied that it was extremely unlikely that he would be in Warrington when the meet- ing took place. It so happened that Mr. Parr was at home, but he wrote stating that the matter was so doubtful that he did not feel he ought to say he should preside, and Mr. Monks kindly consented to take the chair. Mr. Atkin read a letter from Mr. Parr, in which he stated that he had read the annual report with much interest, and considered it very satisfactory. Mr. R. T. Fairclough also wrote regretting his inability to attend. THE REPORT. WARRINGTON'S MUSICAL TASTE. In his annual report the Hon. Secretary stated that the appetite of the public for music of a class worthy of such a society as the Warrington Musical Society was apparently generally feeble, and not only in this town but almost everywhere the taste for oratorio or the concerted music of good composers for platform' performance seemed to exist to such a small degree as to render concert success financially a thing impossible. The difficulty of catering was almost insuperable, and the committee could only hope for a recovery of the healthy appetite to enable it to serve up its dishes with confidence of their being appreciated. At present the selection of any particular work was attended with an enormous amount of speculation as to its reception by an audience. The oratorios "Elijah" and "The Messiah " were no longer certain of attracting an audi- ence anywhere, and many excellent works by modern composers could not be thought of because of the feared financial result. The only feature of change in the usual course of events was the introduction of a specially miscellaneous and chiefly orchestral pro- gramme, including several concerted vocal items by ' members of the society at the final concert on February 21st last. The committee believed this programme to have been heartily approved by those attending the concert. rhe opera section of the society was again most remarkably and deservedly successful in the per- j forwances of "The Gondoliers" in October last,and the I committee was once more conscioue of its debt of ' gratitude to the performers and the Conductor, Opera Committee and all concerned for the invaluable help given to the funds of the society by them. The s successful result of the two operas had enabled the Treasurer to invest a sum of money which was no mean I start for a reserve fund, an object which the committee I had had in view for long, but till now never been able to attempt. The Hoy. TREASURER (Mr. L. W. Reynolds) reported that the loss on the concerts held during the season , amounted to .C4B Ss. 6d. The profit on the opera per- I formances of "The Gondoliers " was £2lB ss. ad., the I amount realized by the sale of tickets being £5ll 2s. 6d. At present the society had a credit balance of £206 19s. 6d. of which £2OO were invested in ,Warrington Corporation Bonds and £6 19s. 6d. was cash in the bank. Mr. W.E. ATKlNmoved and Mr. J. KNOWLES seconded the adoption of the reports. THE MUSICAL TRAINING OF CHILDREN. MR. F. MONKS'S SUGGESTION. The CHAIRMAN said he was very pleased to see the progress that had been made with the orchestral part of the society's work and he would like to see it still further developed. He thought it was very likely that if the Education Committee were app:oached, they would be willing to vote a sum of money to the society for the teaching of elementary instrumental music. That would enable the society to help on that particular part of their work. The reports were adopted. ELECTION OF OFFICERS. Mr. C. WHITE said he had very great pleasure, not ' for the first time, in proposing the election of Mr. J. Charlton Parr as president, for several reasons. The first was that Mr. Parr was very fond of music and had a cultivated taste such as suited the president of a most exemplary society like theirs. He had also given the society his regular support and in that respect he had been an example to his own rank. If every country gentleman in the neighbourhood would support the society in the way that Mr. Parr had done, the society I would not have been obliged to get up those comic operas. They had, however, to take things as they , were. The CHAIRMAN : You don't object to the comic I operas do you ? Mr. WHITR : I don't object to the money (Laughter) I Mr. J. NEWCOMBE seconded. He thought the towns- people were very pleased that the operas were arranged. I They might be rather light for such a society as th.t, but they were very pleasant and also very enjoyable to ' all who took part in them. The proposition was unanimously agreed to. The following vice-presidents were re-elected :—The Mayor, Messrs. Ziles A,mitage, A. H. Crosfield, James Fairclough, John Fairclough, R. T. Fairclough, F. A. Frost, F. Monks, James Menro, Roger C. Parr, C. E. Parker, Colonel Ridgway, L. W. Reynolds, H. Roberts and John White. Mr. W. H. PAYTON moved that Mr. C. White be added to the list of vice-presidents, remarking that he 'had gone a great deal for the cause of music in a quiet -way. Mr. WHITE, however, declined the office. Mr. W. N. Hutchings was elected a vice-president. Later the CHAIRMAN proposed that Mr. Atkin, the retiring secretary, should be elected to the vice- presidency. Mr. J. NEWCOMDE seconded and the proposition met with unanimous acceptance. Mr. ATKIN returned thanks and said he would be pleased to continue to do his best to forward the interests of the society in any capacity. On the motion of Mr.RoG En C. Pa art,seconded by Mrs. W. B. RonsuTe,the committee was elected as follows: Messrs. H. Bond,J. W. Bibby, G. Johnson,J. T. Knowles, .1. Newcombe, P. C.Price,W. Scotson,R. H. Silcock,W. H. Wallington, and R. Whitfield. MR. ATKINS' RESIGNATION. PAST SERVICES RECOGNIZED. Mr. ATKIN said that his arrangements being so unsatisfactorily doubtful he was obliged to resign his position as hon. secretary. The annual meeting was being held later than usual this year and in order to make arrangements for the coming season the committee thought it advisable to elect a secretary to fill his place. Mr. Cyril P. Gough very kindly con- sented to undertake the duties and the committee had, subject to the approval of tbe annual meeting, elected him to the office. It was extremely kind of Mr. Gough to take over the work and he (Mr. Atkin) believed he was exactly the right man for the post. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said he thought it was only right and proper that the meeting should acknowledge by a

formal vote the valuable services Mr.Atkin had rendered (Hear, hear) Those of them who were acquainted with the official work of any society knew that there was always a vast amount of time and attention given to it which was never seen by the public. He was quite certain that there had been much time and devotion to the interests of that society which could never be adequately recognized. He moved that the very cordial thanks of the society be given to Mr. Atkin for his valuable services to the society for so many years. (Applause.) Mr. C. WRITE seconded. He believed the resolution was thoroughly what the meeting ought to pass. They admired Mr. Atkins' courtesy and kindness to all the members, and his willingness to assist the good cause of music in the town. It was a distinct loss that he resigned the secretaryship, and he (Mr. White) was very sorry that circumstances had compelled Mr. Atkin to take that course. They could not have had a better secretary in the interests of the society. (Applause). Mr. F. H. CROSSLEY (conductor of the society) said that for fifteen years Mr. Atkin ha" discharged the duties and probably no one could know better than he (Mr. Crossley) the extent and the difficulty and very often the troublesome nature of the work he bad had to get through, and so often without recognition. The committee had given every assistance possible in the most generous and willing manner, but work of that kind invariably and inevitably fell practically to one person to do: It was not only the knowledge of clerical work that was essential. To make a successful society of that kind so much depended upon other things— urbanity of manner and above all, tact and good temper. He thought every member of the s)ciety must know perfectly well how very much those attributes had entered into Mr. Atkins' administration durinr, the past fifteen years. Mr. Atkin and he had worked together in the greatest harmony and he could only say that it was with great sorrow that he lost Mr. Atkin as a colleague in the inner workings of the society. He could only add that bethought the society was extremely fortunate in its nomination of Mr. Atkins' successor. (Applause.) Mr. NF.WCOMBE, as prob ibly the oldest member of the committee present, endorsed all that had been said. Nothing could have exceeded the tact and good temper Mr. Atkin had shown in his management of the agairs of the society. Ile (Mr. Newcombe) felt sorry for his successor. (Laughter). The vote of thanks was heartily accorded, the chair- man remarking that he was expressing the feeling of the whole of the members of the society when he said they were just as unanimous and appreciative of the services of Mr. Atkin as those present. (Applause). j In acknowledging the compliment Mr. Atkin said it I was hard for him to reply to such a kindly expressed , vote of thanks and he knew the meeting would bear with him if he said that it was almost impossible for him to say exactly what he felt in giving up the work he had done for fifteen years. He thought the society had very fully on many occasions recognised his services and he could perhaps very well have been spared the flattering things said that night. He should very gratefully remember their good feelings. Mr. Crossley and he had been friends for a great many , years and they had worked together with a great deal of pleasure. He was sorry for Mr. Gough, not because he did not think he was quite equal to do what he (Mr. Atkin) had done, but because he had not I the help-meet he (Mr. Atkin) had had. In all his work be had been helped tremendously by his wife, and he hoped she would take to herself some part of the thanks they had lavished upon him. (Applause.) THE NEW SECRETARY. Mr. NEWCOMBE " with much pleasure and heartfelt sympathy "moved the election of Mr. Cyril P. Gough as hon. secretary. Mr.Gough was following an excellent man but he (the speaker) felt sure he would prove nearly if not quite as good a secretary as Mr. Atkin. Mr. F. FIELDHOUSE seconded. If Mr. Gough did as well for the Musical Society generally as ha had done for the opera in particular, they would have a very good successor to Mr. Atkin.
The motion was carried unanimously. THE HON. TREASURER AND OTHER OFFICERS

Mr. PAYTON moved the re-election of Mr. L. W. Reynolds as bon. treasurer, remarking that he was an excellent official, ad entered heart and soul into his work. He also proposed that Mr. Reynolds be cordially thanked for his past services. Mr. KNOWLES seconded the proposition which was carried. Mr. J. NEWCOMBE as re-elected hon. registrar and Mr. W. Johnson librarian, votes of thanks being passed to them for their previous work. MR. CROSSLEY AND THE SEASON'S

div.head: PROGRAMME.
div.p: PROGRAMME.

- ----- Mr. CuossLEv moved a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Monks for presiding. They bad all known him for many years as one of their best supporters and his willingness to come at short notice to take the chair was another evidence of his interest in the society. The arrangements for the coming season were more complete than they had ever been at the corresponding time of any season that he could thing of. The work selected for the first concert was" King Olaf " (Elgar)—a work with which most of them were very charmed on its pre- vious production by the society, the appreciation of the public was as great for that as for any other new work they had ever rendered. There the' several abso- lutely bone fble requests from the public that the society should repeat it. He thought the remarks of Mr. Atkin with regard to the difficulties of the society in the choice of works were particularly good and represented exactly the state of things. He showed how difficult it was to select music that, while it was suitable for a society with such high aims as theirs which did not want to and would not undertake inferior music, would be of equal interest to the public. As years went on, the difficulty increased rather than otherwise, and they were often afraid to tackle a new work for the reasons he had mentioned. Another very serious point was the financial side. Modern works were naturally much more expensive than the old ones to produce. For instance the works of a composer like Eiger required an orchestra double the size of that which assisted in "The Messiah," and it was impossible to supply all the instruments from local resources. The , society would be very much in the fashion by pro- ducing " King Olaf" this season for it was really ' extraordinary to Lind at how many towns it was being undertaken. For the second concert the society would I render" St. John's Eve" (Cowen) with a miscellaneous second part and the third concert would be run on the same lines as the corresponding one last year. It would be of a miscellaneous character and a special feature would be the orchestral items. In conclusion Mr. Crossley heartily thanked Mr. NV. H. Payton for his valuable work as accompanist and Mr. E. H. Pearson for his services as leader of the orchestra. Mr. ATK IN secondeA and added his testimony to the work of the various Officers of the society. The motion was heartily carried and in responding Mr. MosKs said he had always taken a great deal of interest in the society and at one time sang in the chorus. He hoped the society would progress and that that they would have many seasons of delightful music. (Applause.)

div.head: INTERESTING CASE_ AT WIDNES.
div.p: INTERESTING CASE_ AT WIDNES.

Mr. .1. T. Foard, revising barrister, sat at the Widnes Town Hall on Wednesday evening to hear the claims and objections put forth by the political parties. Mr. John Williamson represented the Liberals, and Messrs. E. 0. Evans and E. Muroh the Conservatives. Mr. Williamson put forward seventeen claims, two of which were disallowed, one of these being a claim made by Mr. Louis Cohen, of 104, Widnes-road. Born in Russia, he migrated to Widnes, where he has resided for thirty years. In July 190-1, he applied for his naturalisation papers, but as these did not come to hand until Decem- ber, Mr. Foard could not allow the claim, because Cohen had not been a citizen for the requisite twelve months.—The Conservatives had no claims.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday September 16, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday September 16, 1905.

Know, 1 1,111.yra,, {-ie., la° oreai,- est and loneliest of all our lives. We only seemed to live for Ronny's letters —merry epistles, full of boyish nonsense, with the new wwds in his extensive vocabulary of slang, carefully trans- lated so that we should not lose the point. Every day we would watch the bit of sea that was visi- ble from the side wndow, and if the sun shone and the water sparkled we were very glad, but if the wind howled and the storm clouds hung over the horizon we would both grow strangely sil- ent and miserable, Jane said it was wicked of us, for Ronny was in God's keeping on the ,lea just as much as on land. It was quite true, of course, but it didn't seem to me to lessen the danger of our losing bill). Oh the joy of Ronny's home-coming ! How we laughed and cried by turns over the bronzed and stalwart young lII7M who was so unlike our Ronny, and yet so marvellously like ! How we raved over the gorgeous and utterly useless pre- sents he brought us front the East ! Ronny had grown handsomer than ever in our eyes, and we spoiled him hopelessly. We even allowed him to turn our drawing room, sacred hitherto to our spinster friends, and tuahly• tea-parties, into a smoking-room. Butt it was Ronny, and all he did was right in our eyes. We did lint see so very much of him, after all. He spent a lot of his time at the Magras. We were sorry, of course, but it was only natural. Young men will always go where there are pretty faces and bright eyes to attract them, however fond they may be of the prim old women who have brought them up, and Ronny was no ex- ception to the rule.

'Juno wan quick to see the way things were drifting. "It is Elsie, of course, sister." she said. " I expect that it was for her he brought that ring he showed us the other day." I knew it was Elsie, and I was sorry, but I would not say so to Ronny. because that would only make him all the worse—that in the way with men. Elsie was very pretty, very bright and charming, but she was not the girl I would have chosen for him.
It came about just as we expected. Ronny eame to US ono night to toll us the news. Elsie bad promised to be his wife, he was the happiest of men.
" Just think- of it, Aunt Jane," he said. " That she should love me—it is just too good to be. live."

For ourselves we thought that Elsie had done about the most sensible thing she had ever done in her butterfly life when she fell in love with Ronny. We sympathised with him as well as spinsters could do, arid we asked him to bring Elsie up to tea with Us the next day. We should have liked to keep him to ourselves just a wee bit longer, but when he was 80 happy, who could murmur ? Elsie came up all smiles and blushes, and Ronny was as happy as a king just watching her. We all made a fine fuss over her with which she seemed very well pleased. We did not follow them out in the garden after tea, and we coughed prodigiously and rattled the door handle a great deal when we had to call them for supper. Jane and I consider ourselves admirable gooseberries. It seemed no time before the day canie round for our laddie to be off again. We were heart- broken as usual. Jane always had red eyes for a week before and a week after Ids departure, but I flat ter myself I managed better. Bathing the eyes well in strong Eau-de-Cologne and water may Le extravagant, but it is extremely effectual. This time Ronny was very loth to go. " I can't bear leaving her, Aunt, I really can't," he said on the day preceding him depar- ture. " I have a feeling somehow as if some- thing bad will happen while lam away. It is very foolish, of course, but I cannot help it." Jane and I sympathised with him. We loved him NO much that we thought we could guess what he felt at parting from her. " She will feel it more parting from you," we said sagely. " You will know that she is here, safe at home, and we will look after her for you. But she will have to think of you far away at sea, or in a foreign country, and she will never know what may happen to you.' He laughed heartily

" You 'dear old Aunts," he Raid affectionetely. " When shall I teach you that the sea is as safe RH the hula ? Besides, Elsie is not the one to worry over anything, dear little soul," he added wider his breath, and we thought how wonder- ful a thing was love that could bring such a glad light to his eyes.

But apparently he was right. Elsie never even cried when he left—not openly, certainly, for we took her to Brighton to see hint off. He looked ten thousand times more miserable than she, and his last words as he kissed 11. s good-bye were : " Take care of her, take care of my darling." We promised through our tears, who could help promising anything when he looked so pale and worn ? Then we turned away while they said their good-byes, and only looked again as the train steamed out of the station, and we could see his bonny face so sternly set 4 to hide his grief, while he tried to smile for her sake. Ronny was away more than three years this time, for there was fighting in China, and his ship was in the thick of it, and so was delayed. Nobody can tell what agonies of suspense we went through, or how we sympathised with poor little Elsie. She, poor child, had grown a little pale of late, and had left off many of her laugh- ing, coquettish ways. We used to think her a bit of a flirt, end resent the way in which she went nut driving with one man and another in the neighbourhood, and entertained whole batches of them to tennis in the Rectory garden. Of course the girl may have meant nothing by it, but we were old maids and inclined to be faddy over anything connected with our sailor lad, and we did not like it. But, as I said before, she gave up all these gaieties as the time drew near for Ronny to return, and she became quite grave and edate for her. We thought she too was feeling the suspense, and we pitied her. Then came Ronny's latter asking her to marry him as soon as he landed. He would not have long on shore, lie said, and if they were married immediately, they would be able to spend the whole of it together, and he would be able to see her comfortably settled in her home before he had to leave again. He wrote to us at the same time asking us to use our influence and persuade her to say " yes." It was not a very difficult task. She was quite willing, and if she grew whiter and thinner as her wedding day drew nigh, well, perhaps it was hardly tobe wondered at. There was little enough time to see about her clothes, and Jane and I sat up many a night finishing the house linen. We both hemstitch and do drawn thread work fairly well, and wf had started on an elaborate Outfit as POOll as Ronny left, and the work had helped to pass away many a weary day when the sky hung low on the horizon, and our hearts were sad in spite of our gay talk of Ronny as an admiral. We were finishing the monograms on the very last couple of serviettes when we heard the news. I remember we had got up early in the morning, for we had a lot to do in preparation for the morrow. the glad morrow, the day of Ronny's home coming and his marriage. We were bogt very blithe and merry that sunshiny morning. Jane tried to sing as she sewed, a performance that nearly always provoked my laughter, but that day my heart was too full of prayers for my boy—that and would shield him from pain and unhappiness all his life through. We had done our hest in the paqt, we had tried to keep even the proverbial ertimpled rose leaf from his path. It was bad for him, perhaps, yet we loved to do it. But now 110 had gone beyond us, lie was in God's hands.

div.head: LALL EIGEITS RISSERVED.]
div.p: LALL EIGEITS RISSERVED.]
A LIFE OF SUNSHINE,
DOROTHY BAIRD ,Author of'' 27ie Wooing of Lady !
Was there ever a boy like our sailor lad, I wonder? Could the world ever hold another ..uelt as he? Not for us, anyway—for others perhaps, but never for us. . . .

, . When the letter • came years ago to tell ne that our brother John and his wife had both died Crom cholera, and that his little son with his ayah was coming to us as fast as time and tide and a big steamship could bring him, we were filled with dismay. A boy in our tidy little house ! a boy routing about in our beloved gar- den, where not even a rose petal was allowed to stray from its place ! A. boy shouting and whist- ling at all hours of the day ! it was horrible to think of. Jane wondered dismally how a couple of oh l maids could be expected to know how to rear a child, adding with a sigh that Indian born children are always delicate. I .wondered with equal dolefulness how I could bring myself to imudle an infant, for I Inure always been ner- vous of babies, since my only godchild managed to wriggle itself off my lap and cut its head against the fender. As for talking to a very little thing—it was an impossibility to us. Directly we were confronted by ft " tiny " all words seemed to forsake us. Of course we knew that " Tumtidy-iddity " or nonsense of that sort was the rhtlit way to begin a conversation of that de- scription, but it seemed so ridiculous that we could not bring ourselves to say it. There was another difficulty. What would Sarah Ann say ? Sarah Ann was the " lady " who had condescended to live with us in the capacity of general servant; for the pant eighteen mouths. We felt sure that she would never stay if a child were introduced into the household. She was not a treasure, certainly, but she was better than nothing —or nobody, perhaps I should say —and in these latter days, when good servants seem to be extinct, Jane and I perfectly shud- dered at the thought of receiving a month's notice from Sarah, Ann. It seemed intolerable that we should he put about in this way—the whole tenour of our quiet lives altered —all be- cause of John's baby. We had never approved of his marriage, and we had considered it a tempting of Providence on his part to go and live in Calcutta. Even for the make of a good ap- pointment we thought he had no right to live in an unhealthy place. Well, be had paid the price of his foolishness, but we wondered what we had done that we should suffer for his sins. It seemed a clear fulfilment of the visitation to the third and fourth generation. But such is the way of the world.

All too quickly the day came for Ronny to ar- rive. Sarah Ann, with much slamming of doors and clattering of brooms and pails, accompanied by loud snorts of disapprobation, had prepared the spare room—our only one—for his use. We had dismally enjoyed what we fondly imagined to be our last day of peace wandering up and down the trimly kept paths in the garden, tidy- ing up the sitting rooms with malty regrets that their austerity would soon be marred with toys, even sleeping a little in the afternoon, because we felt sure that the disturbing element would be too strong to allow of such things in the future. But in spite of sighs and dreads the clock ticked on to the appointed hour, and punctually to the minute the cab rolled to the door. Our days of peace were gone for ever. But it was no squealing infant that came into our prim little house, it was no wriggling mass of clothes that confronted us —it was a very brave and bonny boy of two who walked sturdily in, entirely disdaining his Ayah's guiding hands. He did not cry on being confronted by his two sour-faced maiden aunts in their sombre clothing, only his pretty lip quivered, and he asked in lisping accents for his dear mamma._ _

. - Who could resist the piteous pleading in the baby face—the longing of the bonny blue eyes f We weld not. All the Weld motherliness in our cramped-up old hearts went out to him. We al- most quarrelled over who should nurse him, we quarrelled again as to what was good for him to eat at tea, and what was not, we kissed Lim and petted him, till it as a marvel he survived the fervency of our affection. Even Sarah Ann snorted no more, and condescended to call Lim it " blessed bongo]," and net even Jane, always careful to reprove the backsliding, could not bring herself to scold her for applying a heaven- ly name to an earthly being. We had another dispute over who should put him to bed, and yet another as to who should give up her bedroom for his use, for the spare room was a small box of a place, looking towards the dreary north, and we could not think of letting our new-found darling rest there. If Jane went up a dozen times to peep at his rosy face and curly hair as be lsy asleep, [ ant sfraid to say ht)w many times I also trotted up and down the stairs for the saute purpose, or how often we expressed a wish that it were morning, so that we could see the bonny blue of his eyes again. From that time forward Ronny reigned sup- reme at Laburnum Cottage, and we did our best to spoil him— as foolish old maids will. We allowed him to pick our beloved flowers, we loved to see his toys here, there and every where, we enjoyed his merry shouts and innocent prattle. We hard- ly murmured when he broke one of the best tea- cups in his efforts to help Sarah Ann. We near- ly died of fear and anxiety when he.had measles, we never knew a happy moment all the time he had whooping cough. Never shall I forget the agonies of choosing it school for hint, our pride when he brought home a prize, our fears when lie went to a bigger school, our horror when he said —no, I won't write it—a word which we never mentioned even when we came to it in reading aloud to one another. But he was a good boy on the whole, full of mischief, as a boy should be, never tired of playing tricks on poor, adoring Sarah Ann, always getting into scrapes at school, always bringing his friends to help convert the place into a beargarden. But he was an honest, manly little follow, and I think we loved him dl the better for the spice of wic- kedness about him. He never gave us any real trouble, I think, until he announced his inten- tion of going to sett. And that was trouble indeed to us, for we had always sail that we hoped he would never enter the army or navy, for we could not bear to part with our Ronny or to think he was risking his life even for his (ternary. But in spite of our en- treaties he chose the sea, and when once we saw that his mind was made up we said no more, for a man is never happy if he is forced into it pro- fession against his will, and we would never stand in the way of Ronny's lmppiness. So we put our heads together, and practiced various little eCollolllice Si that Ronny should enter the navy and have the best coaching for the exams which /1101IPy could give. Not that we feared he would not pass, we knew he was clever enough for that, but we liked to feel that lie haul the same chances with the highest in the land, and we talked happily to ourselves of the days when he should be an Admiral. We needed to talk of something cheering, for indeed the days were long and dreary all the time he was away, and we dreaded the time when he would be really out on the dreadful, mysterious sea. We (lid not talk of it, however. "Things like that seem to grow worse with talking, but I once caught Jane pulling down the blind at the side window because front it we (solid see a bit of the English Channel between the hills.

As we expected Ronny passed all his examina- tions with the greatest ease, and his mime was so near the top of the list that we thought him a getlius. He came to pay us a long visit before he joined his ship, and we tried to put the thought of his three years exile out of our bends, and en- joYed ourselves thoroughly for the time being. He seemed to us a little graver than he had been before, and be delighted us by saying he wished lo be confirmed before he left.

I never think of Ronny now without thinking of that quiet confirmation Sunday. It was a brilliant day, with not a cloud to break the gor- geous blue of the sky, not a shadow sleeping on the hills. The little church seemed almost dark after the glare outside, but that made it all the more solemn. To us the whole scene became a blurr. We hardly saw the bishop in spite of his crimson robes, we did not notice the girls, or re- mark upon the weirdness of their caps and veils. as had been our godless wont in former days, we did not even look for Elsie Alegre, the rector's beautiful daughter, with her pretty face cm- posed into solemnity for once, and her laughing eyes demurely cast down ; we hardly saw her, even though she almost brushed against Ronny, as he came down and she went up to the bishop. No, we had no eyes for anyone save Ronny, with his pale, stet:Mast face, and the brave look in his eyes as he took his vows which was so good to see. I know I shed many a tear of thankfulness in my corner of our dimly-lighted pew, and I be- lieve Jane did the same, but she will not own to it. How the next three Years nafsed I hardly

tett .tionny r LOW CoURI Re kteur CO see the nil. piness die out of his handsome face, and cold sorrow take its place ? If only it had been something else—if only God had taken one of us —be would not have grieved so much. But Elsie. the one he loved better than all the werh:, the one for whom he had waited so patiently. It was too hard ! We could not trust ourselves to speak of her. A girl who could wait fill, the eve of her mar- riage day, and then run away with another man was beyond our simple comprehension. The ab- solute barbarity of the act filled us with horror. So beautiful and yet so heartless. How could God let such things be? And I had only prayed that morning, oh how fervently ! that our Nadia might be spared all trouble and pain, that he might he happy for evermore. All night long we lay and tossed, counting the weary hours, reckoning up the moments before the awful time when we must stand before Ronny, and tell him that his darling was false, that she had broken her faith, had jilted him on his wedding day. Unrefreshed and heavy-eyed we arose in the morning. If I could have cried I think I should have felt better, but I couldn't. and leaden grief sat all the heavier. We tried to eat our breakfast, but the sobbing Sarah Ann removed the things almost untasted, and then we got ready for our sorrowful journey, for we had decided to meet him at Portsmouth, and had telegraphed to him to come to us at one of the hotels. We thought it might prepare him for bad news, and it would save him from com- ing here, where every turn would remind him of Elsie, if he. would rather go elsewhere.

Never shall I fork.T2t that weary journey. We noted each station with regret an we passed it, and lamented each turn of the wheel because it brought us nearer Ronny, and we bad so longed for, 80 looked forward to his coming ! Ronny was not at the hotel when we arrived, 80 we took off our bonnets and waited, while each of 118 was planning in her mind bow she could put the sad tidings, how she should break tile shock.

At last came tha sound of footsteps in the pas- sage, and my heart leapt to my mouth. The handle turned in the door, but it was only the titer who announced, " Captain Athol." We looked at each other with new dread in our eyes. What could have happened to Ronny ? Captain Athol was a tall and handsome man, he greeted us courteously and gravely, but there was somptltintr in his face which made me clasp my hands in fear. " Yon have bad news, Captain Athol," said Jane, and in Npit.4- of her calm voice, I could see that her lip trembled. He bowed. ••t hardly know how to tell you," he said lamely. _ _
"I think I know," said Jane brokenly. "He is dead. You have come to tell us our boy is dead."
And Captain Athol bowed his bead in silence. . .

They tCiolc us to see him as he lay in his cabin, for he had died in very sight of home, and we held our breath as they drew aside the sheet, and let the morning sunlight chine on 1141 boiiny face, It was very calm, very placid, with the blue eyes closed for ever, but there was a happy expression on it, and the lips were set in a smile of infinite peace. He was like the Ronny who had taken his confirmation Tows in the little old church at home.

So, as we looked, the bitterness of our sorrow passed from us, and the ready tears came to our eyes. Yet they were not wholly tears of grief. God had answered our prayer. Our darling would never know the truth, and be had passed untroubled into the everlasting joy of heaven.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THEFT FROM THE MARKET.

At Warrington on Monday Elizabeth Cooper, 11, Roger-street,lwas charged with stealing a pair of corsets value 15.6 d., the property of Margaret Blakeley.—The Chief Constable stated that on Saturday night tbe prisoner was seen in the marketaccorapanied by a little girl about four years of age. She was seen to knock a pair of gloves off a stall, which were picked up and handed to her by the little girl. The attention of the proper authorities was called to the woman and the gloves were taken away from her. Later in the even- ing a market inspector saw the prisoner knock a pair of corsets off a stall. These were also handed to her by the little girl, and she placed them under her coat. When stopped and questioned she indignantly denied having stolen the corsets,saying that her girl had picked them up. The presence of the little girl was a particu- larly had feature.—Prisoner was fined 10s. including costs. _

div.head: AN IMPORTANT CAPTURE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: AN IMPORTANT CAPTURE AT WARRINGTON.

Some time ago two men named Davies and High= were sent to gaol by the Warrington magistrates for six months each for stealing block tin value £lO, the property of the Whitecross''Company, Ltd. On Tuesday Wm. Blanchard was brought before the magistrates on a charge of being implicated in the theft.—Mr. T. S. Steel stated that on the night of the 15th July the watchman in the employ of the prosecu tors caught Davies near the warehouse from which the tin had been extracted. Davies implicated Higham and Blanchard, but Blanchard for some time evaded arrest. The previous day P.C. Metcalf saw him walking along Sankey-street, and recognizing him as being wanted in connection with the affair arrested him. Prisoner at first tried to bluff the officer hut sub- sequently admitted his guilt. He (Mr. Steel) pressed- for the infliction of a severe penalty.—The Chief Con- stable described the arrest as an important on. Since the conviction of Davies and Iligham and the absence from town of the prisoner the robberies from works in the town had absolutely ceased. Blanchard had been sent to prison for three months on a previous occasion for stealing lead from a local works.—Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was sent to gaol for six mouths with hard labour. SERIOUS CIIARGE AGAINST A PUBLICAN.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday., before Messrs. J. C. Parr (in the chair), John White, H. Nield, F. Monks,'and Colonel Ridgway, John Henry Kirby, of the Millstone Inn, Whitley Superior, was summoned for haying on the 13th August, permitted drunkenness on his licenses premises. Mr. W. H. Churton, of Chester, prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. Author Browne, of Warrington, defended. Mr. Churton said that at about 9.40 on August 13th, P. C. Bostock,visited the Millstone Inn and found ten Irish farm labourers outside, eight in the lobby of the house and ten English- men in the bar parlour. James Drury, one of the men standing in the lobby, was drunk and noisy. Drury it appeared went to the house at 12.30 and remained there as long Its he could with other Irish farm labourers, and had iiV3 pints of beer. So far as he knew there were no reasonable precautions taken 7 and the licensee's mother seemed to have supplied the men with as much drink as they chose to ask for. Witnesses were called in support of this statement.— Mr. Browne said that Drury went into the house per- fectly sober between seven and eight in the evening, and the landlord served him with four pints of hem Drury was not drunk, and was capable of taking care of himself. The defendant saw no signs of drink about the men and there was nothing in their appearance to attract his attention. The defendant had an unblemished character. He had kept a house in Crewe for four years and a half without a conviction, and that was saying a great deal, and he was with the London and North- Western Railway Company for 12 years. Evidence hav- ing been given for the defence. The Bench retired to consider their decision, and when they returned the Chairman said they had decided to dismiss the case.

"Guard of Honour" Soldiers at Warrington. Last week-end Warrington was visited by 150 men and two bands of the 2nd Battalion King's Livefpool Regiment from Aldershot. The soldiers arrived on Friday afternoon and proceeded- to Orford Barracks ! where arrangements had been made for their accom- modation. The primary object of their visit to : Lancashire was to form a guard of honotir at the unveiling of the memorial erected in Liverpool to their comrade who lost their lives in the, Afghan, Burmese and South African wars. Sir George White, the gallant defender of Ladysmith, performed the ! ceremony on Saturday in the presence of a vast I assembly. On Sunday morning the Guard of Honour and bands accompanied the soldiers stationed at the depot to the Parish Church for the usual service. On returning the bands plays choice selections on the Siplare at the Barracks. The public were admitted i and greatly enjoyed the programme. The men returned to Aldersbot at 9.15 on Monday morning.

MY DEAR CHILDREN, I am pleased to tell you that the lists of new members bave been coming in very well during the last few weeks. Next week I will give you full particulars of the Watch Com- petition. In the meanwhile I will tell you that the prize has been awarded to Ernest Doney. The list is certainly very good, and I congratulate him on his energy in getting such a large number of new members. We have now passed the 300th. Florence Prescott has been awarded a prize volume, the above being„ her "Children's Corner" number. I hope, Florence, that this book will not be the last one that I shall send you. The Prize Winner for Solution of Puzzles is Alice Long. You will remember that I asked my young friends to send me letters. Well, I have received several during the last week.
You will see by the following that my nephew is looking forward to next year and intends to grow flowers. I am pleased to hear this:—
sear Long Sutton, Lines.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending in the answers to puzzles. I have not been able to get many names, as we live in an out-of-the- way place. I have got my garden dug, raked, and some suitable manure put in it. I intend to grow flowers in it. I also have another larger one in which to grow cabbages and turnips for my rabbits in winter. I was glad to see so many more names in the "Children's Corner." _

ICHE RUBBER PLANT AND THE PALM. A Rubber-plant and a small Palm stood Upon a parlour floor. From either side the fire-place They scanned each other o'er.
"What do you rub?" the small Palm asked - His statelier neighbour tall. ' "Alas l" the Rubber-plant replied, "I cannot rub at all.
" If I had hands, like yours," he said, As wiEtfully he eyed His smaller neighbour's pretty palms With fingers opened wide.
" Then I could rub 1 "—" And yet," replied The little Palm, "you see, Though I have hand.% I can not rub, And that's the rub.with me.
"I wonder why it's always so: That something we have got Seems never quite complete to be, Without what we have not.
"I've often longed to rub my hands With glee, here in my tub; And you, no doubt, have often wished You had some hands to rub.
"Now, if you were I, or I were you,— No, that's not right, I see,— But if you and I, were you or I, What a fine plant we should be I"
Still, they did as all good plants should— Kept green all winter long; So no one ever knew or guessed That anything was wrong.

A NARROW ESCAPE. A TRUE INCIDENT. (Continued.)
"We'll take him home and make a pet of him," said Tom. "Mother would rather see a string of fat birds, or a deer," said Harry; "but for us, this is the best find we could have."

It was not so easy to get young Bruin away as they had supposed it would be. They found belts and strings on their clothing, and in their pockets but they had to give the little fellow some liberty or he would nave broken away. At last they concluded to carry him; but he struggled so they did not get on very fast.

"Oh, Hal 1" Tom suddenly screamed, drop- ping the cub, "there's the mother!" Sure enough, Mamma Bear had missed her baby from her warm winter nest and was coming after him in a great rage. Tom raised his gun and fired. The ball entered the bear's shoulder, wounding her slightly. Furious with pain, she sprang upon Tom and began tearing at him with her claws and trying to crush him against her shaggy bosom. Little Harry stood for an instant paralyzed with fear. He knew that if he should fire, he was as likely to kill his brother as to kill the bear. Yet, Tom's only hope was in what,,the little brother could do.
Harry crept up beside the bear, and fired. The next instant the bear and Tom were lying in the snow, which was deeply stained with blood.
• "Oh, Tommy!" cried Harry, "are you dead?"

"No; but roll the bear off or I'll smother," came from Tom's white lips. Harry touched the bear cautiously, but she made no resist- ance; the ball had entered her brain and killed her instantly. Tom tried to give his little brother a good hug to show his joy at being alive, but he found his arms were so wounded in places that he was in great pain, and feared that his shoulder was broken, also. "Don't cry, after you've been such a man," he said, for Harry was sobbing aloud over his brother's wounds.
"The cub shall be yours, 'cause you got so hurt in getting him," said Harry, wiping his eyes. . _At

"No, he's yours, 'cause you kept mr. from being killed altogether. I won't fling your being slim at you any more, for you can shoot as well as the strongest kind of man!" This praise made Harry feel equal to any- thing, even to dragging away the unwilling cub. The little fellow sniffed around his mother, whining piteously. But Harry was a strong boy in spite of his slender build, and Tom gave what help he could in his enfeebled condition. Little Bruin was as "hungry as & bear," so the lunch in Tom's bag was a great help in bringing him along. When they reached the camp they found the men at dinner. The " boss " ordered one of them to take the boys home on a wood-sled. But the boys insisted on taking their fallen game with them; so while Tom's wounds were bound up, after a fashion, and both boys were being well fed, some of the men went after the old bear. Mrs. Brown's liking for hunting was not in- creased when the sled stopped before her door, with a dead bear, a live, bear, and a wounded boy. Torn bore the docter's stitches and his con- finement so well, however, that she at last gave her consent to have the cub kept for a play- mate. The old bear's skin was sent to Mar- quette to-be sold, and the boys treated all their friends to bear's meat.

"Browny" has become a great pet. Even the boys' mother cannot but admit that he is full of .amusing tricks. I believe there is a bright future for our bold young hunters. In time they will be brave and good men. But Browny acts more and more like a bear every day, and soon he will be altogether too big to be considered a pet.

Played at St. Helens, before a poor attendance. Traynor started for St. Helens, and after a brief incur- sion to the Morecombe end the visitors took up a foot- ing in the borne half. Traynor and Johnson attempted passing, but G. Wilson intercepted Traynor's pass, and scored a rather easy try, the goal kick failing. More- cambe again made headway, and the home defence I was subject to severe pressure for some time. St. Helens eventually got into the Morecambe half, where Prescott picked up, and scored a splendid try under the posts for Traynor to improve. Creeney shortly after made a grand run, and threw to Johnson, who got in at the corner. Traynor failed to improve Morecambe again got dangerous, and from a cross kick by Banks, Beech nearly got in. Near the interval Creeney again scored, and Lea converted. Half-time score :—St. Helens 2 goals, 3 tries (13 points), More- cambe 1 try (3 points). On the resumption G. Play after favoured the a Saints," who literally carried everything before them Toole commenced with dropping a goal, and then Banks Prescott and Lea added tries, Traynor improving the first one. no matter what improvements were atteropt• in human conditions. No doubt he conceived It to be the truth, but. all experience since his time has been against it ; and now, many coun- tries are crying out for Population. The doc- trine or a permanently fixed nimery and starva- tion boundary was one to sap the energies of re- formers' and to make those who longed for th gradual improvement and prosperity of the race to feel hopeless and despairing. It has so acted. The effect of the Malthusian doctrine, as usually understood or misunderstood, has been so evil, that in spite of the high character of its author, I think it ought to be stionatised as a foul lie, and a libel on humanity.

THE PRESENT PHASE OF THE STRUGGLE. There are those who think that only by main- tenance of the Darwinian struggle for existence can the human race be kept in the path of ener- gy and progress ; that if the keenness of compe- titive struggle were suspended, or even lessened, a reaction of inertia and decay and degradation would set in.

That activity and enterprise and initiation, mid struggle in one sense, are necessary, is cer- tainly true, but it need not be competitive struggle. The effort that must be made may be an effort to help our fellows, to succour the weak and the distressed, not to trample them down and rise by standing on their bodies. It were a ghastly parody if we rose to higher things only by stepping stones made of the dead selves of other people. The success of one which is only attainable by the failure of others is a poor thing. Progress, learning, wisdom, which are distributive and assimilable by all, are the really worthy noble things now. We. are, as men, beyond the struggle for exis- tence now ; we have entered on the era of co- operation and mutual help. We can control the forces of nature. We have not any longer to adapt ourselves to an environment : we can amend it; we can make our own environment. We are driven by the lash of no blind necessity; we can choose the good and eschew the evil, or we can choose the evil and forsake the good. Our destiny is largely in our own hands: we have become as gods.
