SIR OLIVER LODGE (Principle if Bironinghain trniversity:

In a right condition of society the ethical state of adults should be higher and more ad- vtuiced than that of children, on the average ; that is to say training and experience of life should have improved them. With us at present I believe it is the reverse, and. that children, on the average, are born into the world better than in a few years they become; the majority seem to have suffered deterioration, not eleva- tion, from their social surroundings • their training has on the whole been bad. I hope that this may be false, but if it be true it is a grievous indictment against the conditions un- der which we live.

div.head: IMPILOTED PUBLIC INSTITUTES.
div.p: IMPILOTED PUBLIC INSTITUTES.

I would have social institutes with large pub- lic rooms, games, entertainments—anything that the people could provide for themselves, or that might be provided for them—and leave them ' to the good sense and natural feelings of each other. Subject to actual experience under good conditions in the opposite directions, I should say: Let drink of every kind be pro- vided for sane adults, but let there be food also, and let there be no profit on the drink, especial- ly not on alcoholic drink, to those who retail it. Let it be obtainable, but not too easily and ob- trusively obtainable, nor in any way forced upon people. There is no sense in the present sys- tem, whereby over-drinking is encouraged as the only way to secure good fellowship and comfortable housing during the hours of play. There are the theatres, it is true—where people are crowded, uncomfortably, relegated to back seats, and with the liability to have to stand in queues for a long time before the doors are open. This is a horrible waste of time. If thea- tres are not crowded at the present day they dc not " pay." This necessity for " pay is de- trimental to any form of art. There ought to be at least ore Municipal theatre where' there shall be room and comfort for all, at low prices, with- 'out necessarily having to go in at the beginning; or long before the beginning, and where rea- sonable plays can be exhibited and songs sung, even if they do not attract constantly crowded houses. The entertainment and recreation of the people after their day's toil is too import- ant a matter to be left wholly to private enter- prise ; it is not a thing that should be exploited by individuals for private gain : that is not the way to secure entertainments of a high class. The supply of intoxicating liquor also is not a mat- ter that should be conducted for private profit ; it is too serious a thing for the welfare ot a na- tion. A man who has laboured hard all day with his body is naturally thirsty ; he requires li- quid, and in this climate he imagines that he requires some stimulant. I sympathise with him, but whether he is right or wrong it is ex- tremely little use coercing or restraining his body without controlling or guiding his intel- ligence and will ; unless indeed he is already in a diseased condition. Too many are in that condition, but the young surely are not, and there lies our hope ; a new generation may be brought itp under wholesomer and more natural conditions, and the deadly, diseased craving for over-doses of any form of drug, instead of having to be curbed and eradicated, need never originate.
MUNICIPAL ENTERTAINMENTS.

At these municipal places of entertainment, reasonable food and drink and music should be freely accessible, and public opinion should be left gradually to contenm excess. Depend upon it the habitual drunkard would not seek these open and airy and public places for gratifica- tion of his vice ; be would retreat into the slums, there to further contaminate his depraved or- ganism with the material which, by physiologi- cal necessity, it now demands. Many of these unhappy people doubtless in their saner mo- ments wish to be reclaimed, and there are plenty of agencies for that work: That is not the kind of work on which I wish to speak. My main' point is that average and undiseased people should be drawn and not pushed, attracted to- wards the better and not driven from the worse ; that forcible compulsion is a poor way of deal- ing with a free agent, and that influencing and attracting the mind is far better than restricting, and compelling the body ' • that municipal Go- vernment may wisely aim at more activity that is positive, so as gradually to diminish the need , for so much that is negative. I am convinced that drunkenness Is largely due to the misery and poverty and monotony and grimy hopelesa- ness and practical homelessness in which so many people live ; they have no outlook upon life, and they have few home comforts they enter a " works " on leaving school, and they stay in that or siinilar works, doing some simple task continuously, and earning a weekly wage, except on holidays, and when they are ill, and when for any reason they are un- able to work, right away to the end of life. Their labour is often fearfully monotonous, though it is true that gradually their sensitive- ness becomes atrophied so that they do not feel it so. Nevertheless it is 83, and the monotony must have a deteriorating effect on themselves as human beings not machines. Their salvation would be to have some hobby, some home inter- est, even some home, something to look forward to each evening, each week, each year, and, if possible, something to look forward to when they get old. At present what they appear to look forward to is either the pecuniary excitement of a race, or witnessing and betting on a football match, or else what they call a" booze." It is a dismal existence, and it is difficult for the peo- ple immersed in it to scheme themselves out of it, or to organise a better. That duty lies upon us, and upon those leaders of industry in whose system the existence of people of th is kind is be- lieved, perhaps erroneously, to be of service and to be commercially beneficial. It is a conveni- ence to them that there should be people willing to go through these humdrum tasks for long hours every day • it is a convenience to them %nit there should be a certain number of people standing idle waiting to be hired whenever a vacancy occurs ; many of these things are or appear to be conveniences, but they are pur- chased at a high price • and one price, which should be recognised, is that employers should feel themselves bound, either separately or in combination, to see that wholesome habitations and human conditions are provided for all who are or may be their workpeople.
MORE COMFORT-MORE TRADE.

Raising the standard of comfort, increasing the atmosphere of self-respect, introducing some hope and pleasure into life, will do more than much preaching to diminish drunkenness ; it will likewise be commercially profitable, for it will increase the demanding power of the people for goods ; it will therefore increase trade and manufacture, especially manufacture of • things of a better class. At Present the purchasing power of the people is far too small ; conse- quently a great litter of cheap rubbish has to be provided, and we have to seek foreign markets for many of our best goods ; but if only we could develop the home market, make the whole populace able to demand things, and to buy things, and to use things, then the wealth of the country would increase i in compound inter- est fashion. Every worker who is also a pur- chaser increases his fellows' chances of employ- ment at the same time that he provides for them things useful and desirable.
STIMULOtiS TO WORK.

The raising of the standard of comfort for the average man and the average family must go much further than it has at present ; it will help to raise people out of their present low condi- tion, it will do more to really civilise them, than almost anything else. People do not work well for bare necessities ;. they work well for ideals, for aspirations, for comfort, yes for luxuries. The whip of starvation is not the necessity nor the assistance that it used to be thought ; it is no better than the whip of the slave-driver— and best work was never yet got out of slaves. Employers who profit by the dire norprty and huger of their workers are the loathiy crew called sweaters. There never was a ghastlier mistake than that made by Malthus, if he ever said, what be is usually interpreted to have said, that the population of the earth must al- ways increase until restricted by the leek of the means of subsistence ; in other words, that starvation was the necessary condition of human life at its margin, that there would always be a residue on the verge of death by starvation, whatever was done 110 help them, and that people would btop4 11,,t2 &1,1 tnta of thittaa obfftined.

div.head: BEAUTIFYING STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: BEAUTIFYING STOCKTON HEATH.
Tree-Planting Committee Formed.

I Stockton Heath is to be further beautified by the ' planting of trees in various parts of the village. The residents are taking up the matter with enthusiastism ! and at a largely attended public meeting held in the Hall Cafe, -Victoria Square, on Tuesday evening a I scheme was adopted and a committee appointed to carry it out. Mr. Vere B. Davies presided. Mr. A. Fawcett, hon. secretary of the Garden Society which has initiated the movement, read letters from Lady Greenall,. Mrs. Lyon, and Mr. P. Egerton- Warbuiton expressing warm approval of the scheme. Lady Greenall hoped that the society would also encourage the planting of creepers on the houses. The Chairman said he should be pleased to assist in any way he could in the movement, because he thought the idea of planting trees was an excellent one in every way, and nothing added so much to the beauty of a place as trees, shrubs and flowers. Any place might be made beautiful by the planting of laburnums, lilacs, and hawthorns, but he was sorry to say that in the present day there was an unfortunate tendency on the part of 1 the British public to pull trees to pieces and to cut ' names on them. He suggested that it would be a good thing if each schoolmaster and schoolmistress would I inculcate in the minds of the children under their care respect for the beautiful, and the general public might do a great deal to help in keeping the trees in good I order by reporting any act of damage that was done. ' (Hear, hear). Mr. Fawcett read the scheme drawn up by the com- mittee as follows :—The committee suggest that the scheme of tree planting, and in other ways beautifying the village, shall commence at Victoria- square as a centre. That from a point at the Ifront of the Hall Cafe six trees be planted, ten yards apart in the direction of Grappenhall-road, join- ing up to the existing trees planted there. That from ' the above-named point, running toward the corner up I London-road, to a point near Mr. Knight's shop, 16 trees be planted. That Mr. Warburton be asked to plant shrubs (rhododendrons, Ste.), in the ground enclosed by the railings. That in front of the police station in Grappenhall-road two trees be planted. That the Parish Council be asked to put a curb, defining a foot- path, at the side of the Polies Station facing across the front of the Mulberry Tree Hotel, and that three trees be planted on each footpath. That cox the footpath in front of Mr. Turton's shop, facing the square, two trees, or shrubs' planted in tubs, be placed. That leave be obtained to plant three trees in Mr. Unsworth's garden in Walton-road. That in front of Mr. Speakman's and the shops below two trees be planted. That in Dundonald- avenue three trees he planted on each side,ten yards apart, the first on each side being at the corner of the street- entrance from Walton-road. That in front of Mr.Welsby's at the corner of Kimberley-drive one tree be planted, and three more,towards the square,each ten yards apart. I That on the opposite side of Mr. Welsby's in Kimber- I ley-drive, three trees be planted, the first at the corner of Walton-road, and two on tie opposite side, the first I one being ten yards from the tree at the corner. From i Kimberley-drive in Walton-road towards Whitefiel d road, two be planted inside the walls of the garde there. That one tree be planted in the garden occupid by Mr. Vernon. That at the junction of Whitefiel road with Welton-road the seats surrounding the tre already pl anted there, be removed and re-placed else where on the green, and substantial railings erecte round as much ground as permission can be obtained to enclose. Such ground to be raised in a bank up to the 1 tree, as a centre, and planted with shrubs. Also that I the Parish Council be asked to surround the ground with a curb. That the trees be planted, where possible, ten yards apart—planted in good and proper soil, and fenced. That those wishing to have a tree planted opposite their own houses, at their own expense, shall be urged to agree to have such trees planted in a position that will not interfere with the carrying out of a complete scheme. The total expense is estimated at £52. Mr. J. H. Clarke proposed that a society be formed to plant trees for the purpose of beautifying the district. He had advocated a similar scheme for some years, as Stockton Heath lent itself particularly to it. Chelten- ham was one of the most beautiful towns he had ever seen. There was a magnificent street in it, with no fewer than four avenues. They might also have a village decorating society. Mr. H. J. Westbrook asked the meeting to look at the matter from the utilitarian point of view. No doubt the scheme would be carried, but who would look after the trees ? Why had Whiteneld-road been left out? (Laughter.) The maintenance of the trees was an important consideration. All they wanted was a committee of the Garden Society to carry out the movement, and it would not be respectful on the part of the meeting to ignore that society. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Clarke said there was no intimation from the Garden Society that they were willing to take the matter in hand. If they were willing they would have his supporti and he would also help them financially. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. H. Woodcock said the Garden Society had considered the matter and had secured numerous promises for the planting of trees, and it was not therefore, likely they would neglect their work. They , did not expect all the trees to be planted in a year, or that Stockton Heath would blossom out all it Once like Cheltenham, Bournemouth and other places. The scheme was only a partial one and they had stopped at Whiteflold-road because it was respectable already, and because some of the residents there might be induced to look after their gardens first. (Laughter.) They wanted tree-planting day in Stockton Heath to be quite an institution. (Applause.) There would be no necessity to appoint another society as it would be a weakness rather than a strength. (Hear, hear.) After further discussion. The Rev. H. V. PIGOT proposed a resolution to the effect that the meeting approved of the scheme as sub- mitted to them by the Garden Society, and desired it to be carried into effect. Mr. E. Bradshaw seconded, and the motion • was unanimously carried. On the motion of Mr. Woodcock, seconded by Mr. ' Bradshaw, it was further decided that the Garden I Society Committee, which consists of twelve, be part of the Tree-planting Committee in addition to Mr. J. W. Bouchier, (chairman of the Parish Council), Mr. J. H. Clarke, Mr. Tandy, Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, Mr. W. Mclntyre, Mr. H. J. Westbrook,Mr. John Hallows, and Mr. John Mynekyme. I Mr. Fawcett announced that twenty-one parishioners had promised trees and be thought that was a good start (Applause). Subscriptions had also been received in support of the expenses. It was decided to leave the date of tree-planting for the decision of the committee.

CHARGE AGAINST A WARRINGTON COAL DFALITR, At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Samuel I Shaw, coal dealer, Warrington, was summoned for offer- ing for sale a 4uanity of coal of less weight than was specified on the label. inspector Hind said that on July 28th, he saw the defendant delivering coal at a house in Walton road, Stockton Heath. He weighed six of the bags and they were found to be eleven pounds altogether deficient in weight. Mr. Steel appeared for the defendant, and stated that there were only eleven pounds short out of 6721b5. The coal was weighed previous to leaving the yard, and pieces might easily have fallen off. The magistrates dismissed the case on payment of costs—Thomas Shaw, father of the defen- dant in the last case was summoned for having in his possession a pair of scales which were unjust. Inspector Hind stated that on July 28th he endeavoured to weigh the coal, but was unable to do so, as the scales were out of order and were unjust. Mr. Steel stated that the scales were examined by the Warrington inspector only a month ago. The defendant had no knowledge that the machine was out of order. He was a most respect- able man, and no complaint had ever been made against him before. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed,

div.head: Wages of Corporation Workmen.
div.p: The Wages of Corporation Workmen.

Sir,—The rpectacle of men enjoying the comforts and luxuries of life mostly, if:not altogether, through , the labours of their humbler brethern, refusing even a ' living wage to workmen under their control is one that is boundte excite suspicion as to their justice and I humanity, and fitness to excite power over others. Such a spectaclas was witnessed in the Town Hall at the debate on the wages question which you reported in the " Examiner " of last Saturday. On that occasion Councilkr Stott ventured to introduce a modest resolu- tion to ay all Corporation workmen over 21 years a minimum wage of 21s, a week. But in an assembly of Christian men (for I am bound to assume that all our local solons are Christians or at least members of churches and chapels) the modest proposition was re- ceived with amazement, opppsition and even laughter, and only six members had the courage to support it. The other members present seemed to think that it was extravagant, that it would increase the rates, and lead to a rush of miserably paid labourers from the surround- ing manufacturies to the Town Ball. They preferred to keep things as they are, and pay their humble but useful and necessary employees at rates lower than those expended on paupers and criminals ! What a sickening contrast this conduct presents to the gracious •zttitude which the Council assumes when the Town Clerk, Borough Surveyor, Rate Collector or ,other highly paid servant of the ratepayers, ask 'for an increase of wages ! A faint imitation of opposition is sometimes offered, but it is Instantly overborne by the approving Aldermen and their friends who, of course, consider themselves the only competent persons to appraise the superlative merits of the higher class of employe. I dare not impugn the wisdom and justice shown on these occasions but I may be permitted to remark that, with the great ability at their service the Corporation should be so often in a muddle as they seem to be, is passing strange. The echoes of the trading inquiry are still lingering in our ears while irregularities connected with the water department are forming matters for heated discussions in the Council. It is alleged that a contract for £24,000 has somehow developed in an expenditure of £57,000. If an investigation takes place it is to be hoped that it , will not be so farcical as was the one about the Mayor and Councillors' trading with the Council. The paying of low wages is one of the prime causes which, lead to the poverty which darkens so many of the homes of the working classes and limited liability companies, large and small, and other employers of labour are responsible for it. Selfish and ambitious men whose only aim in life seems to be building up fortunes for themselves and their posterity at the cost of the toil and suffering of their fellow creatures are on the increase and were it not for the intervention of Trade Unions the lot of the workers would be much worse than it is. The Corporation of Warrington in its dealings with its humble workmen is a faithful imitator of the methods of the Company Director and his drivers. Yours truly, lONA. September, 1905. -

div.head: Labour Reprasentation.—An Anomaly.
div.p: Labour Reprasentation.—An Anomaly.

Sir,—Much has been said and written from time to time concerning the attitude adapted by the Labour Representation Committee towards the candidate for Parliamentary honour. It may be considered ungracious for an outsider to critcise the actions of such a body, but for one who has been more than a casual observer of the onerous work which it has set itself to accomplish and who is cognisant of the difficulties which beset it on all sides, a little friendly criticism may not be altogether out of place. Working for the common good, even gratuitously, is oft' times an unpleasant occupation. There are more hard knocks than thanks. It may be that, like unto the villian in the piece, the hisses are the criterion by which one measures the amount of good accomplished. It is not necessary to refer to recent local events, and the ploughire, of the lonely furrow attitude which a certain respected Labour Councillor advised his friends to adopt: a striking illustration of the practical bearing of what I have been induced to allude to has happened within the last few days. Perhaps," The Editor" will allow me to make use of three newspaper cuttings which will explain and exemplify the point raised ; but before doing so a little explanation is necessary. Men possessing only ordinary business training, and its accompanied activity, would experience little diffi- culty in believing that the Labour Representation Committee, by upholding the clearly defined rules which it has set itself to work by, was, whatever may be said against the rule, honest to itself so long as it conscientiously adhered to them. There can be no mistake as to the purport of them. No candidate can be accepted by that committee if he is a member of the Liberal or Conservative bodies. I think that is a fair statement of the case. I shall not say anything further than that at present. Now let us see what is being done in the North of Ireland and we will let the "cuttings "speak for themselves : The Labour Leader Ist September, 1905. NORTH BELFAST ELECTION. A CHANCE FOR LABOUR. By the death of Sir James H. Ha.slett, the North Division of Belfast loses its Par- liamentary representative, and gives an oppor- tunity of industrial Ireland to speak its mind on the subject of Labour Representation. Mr. William Walker, the district delegate of the Carpenters' and Joiners, Society, is the nominee of the local Labour Party as candidate for the Divi- sion. He has been adopted by the L.R.C., and by his own society by an almost unanimous vote—a striking tribute to his popularity, in view of the fact that his public work has been chiefly confined to Belfast, while only a small fraction of the mem- bers of his society are resident in Ireland. The light will be a hot one, of that there can be no doubt in the mind of anyone who knows Belfast. But the Labour Party are going to win. They have the advantage of being first in the field, having already distributed Mr. Walker's election address to every elector, held several meetings, and got a systematic canvass well under weigh, before the other candidate has been adopted." " The Labour Leader," Bth, September, 1905. The Independent Labour Party demonstration in Hanley on Monday evening was a large success. Disappointment was felt at the absence of J. R. Macdonald, owing to the absolute necessity for his presence at the Belfast bye-election. "The Daily News," 13th, September, 1905. L.R.C. " UNIONIST "CANDIDATE. We do not understand the position of the Labour candidate in the bye-election now going on in North Belfast. In his election address Mr. Cone- oilier W. Walker rightly enough points out: As a Labour candidate, selected at a conference in the engineers' hall, representative of practically every organization in the city, convened by the Belfast Labour Representation Committee, my position is one that calls for full and fair consider- tion at your hands. There we agree. But is Mr. Walker within the letter of the L.R.C. constitution in the next para- graph of his address ? This is how it begins : AS A UNIONIST in politics. I can recognise that those who are not such may be equally honest in their deiire to promote the welfare of Ireland. The only other candidate is Sir Daniel Dixon. He, too, is appealing to the electors "as a Unionist in politics. Mr. Walker is so proud of being a Unionist that he prints the announcement iu black capitals, although he is content with ordinary type in the previous paragraph, that describes him as the Labour candidate. What would happen if one of the L,R.C. candidates described himself in his elec- tion address as a Liberal in politics? Would it not be well that the Self-Denying Ordinance should apply all round? The position in Belfast is probably unique. "A Unionist in politics" is there being supported by the Labour Representation Committee and which has allowed its own secretary to go over and help on the candidature. There must be some explanation for these remarkable proceedings by such an august Committee and it is awaited by—Yours truly,
NUNQUALM.

Crosftelds' Anglers' Association. The distribution of prizes in connection with this Society's competition, took place in the Works' I Assembly Room on Friday last. The Chairman stated that they had entered two teams for the War- rington Association's Challenge Shield, and that the Committee had decided to hold another competition in about a fortnight. Mr. Roberts, the President of the Association, in presenting the prizes, announced that he would again give the first prize when this competi- tion took place. He was pleasea. to see that the Fishing Section at the works was making great pro- 1 gress, and was being supported by so large a number of workmen. In a few well-chosen worth, he con- gratulated the 14 prize winners, and held out encouragement to the 89 other competitors. The prizes, which were substantial and tastefully selected, included :—First, T. Clair, marble clock ; second, W. Hudson, silver teapot ; third, J. Holden, silver cruet ; fourth, A. 0 verend, rod and reel; fifth, J. Payne, carvers ; sixth, E. Emery, silver guard and medal. The meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to the President, which was moved by Mr. ewall and seconded by Mr. Lord and which Mr. Roberts acknowledged in graceful terms.

div.head: WATERWORKS' CONTRACT,
div.p: THE WATERWORKS' CONTRACT,
MEETING OF RATEPAYERS IN THE PARR HALL.
Councillor Pemberton's Action Approved.
ALARM AT THE CONTRACTORS CLAIM.
" Regaining Warrington's Honour."

There was a large attendance at the Parr Hill on Thursday evening at a meeting called by the Non- Trading Association of "ratepayers favourable to the action of amacillor Pemberton and his colleagues in the Town Council in regard to Lawson's Water Contract and other matters." Mr. James Dodds presided and was supported on the platform by Councillors Pemberton, Lord, Ashcroft, Benson, and Skelland, and Messrs. S. Norbury Williams (Man- chester) S. Kenyon, H. Thornton and Alfred Halme.

The dHAIRMAST, Who was very heartily received, said : I had hoped that our gathering of eleven months ago at which we welcomed and thanked our three Inquiry Commissioners for their splendid services in the cause of public probity would have been our last. But the con- duct of the Water Committee during the past few months and finally of the Council itself, has rendered it imperative that we should again confer with you in this way, and ask

div.head: YOUR FREE_AND OPEN JUDGMENT
div.p: YOUR FREE_AND OPEN JUDGMENT

and verdict upon the issues involved; a verdict as to the character of which after you have heard Mr. Coun- cillor Pemberton, I have no doubt whatever. You may not be aware, but it is the fact, that for nearly three years, that is ever since his election as a member of the Water Committee, Mr. Pemberton has been vainly endeavouring to get such information in regard to its contracts, and more especially in regard to the Lawson contract,as he required and such as he was fully entitled to under the Standing Orders of the Council. The Standing Orders are the rules under which the mem- bers of the Council work, and within which they are entitled to claim to work. Standing Order No. 37 reads:—
"That every member of a Committee shall be entitled at any time to inspect all books, papers and documents, and shall at all times have access to

all the works and undertakings of such Committee." As a member of the Water Committee Mr. Pemberton has been almost continually asking for an inspection of the agreement, the specification, accounts, and other' documents appertaining to the Lawson Water Contract. This contract was signed on the 21st September, 1900, and has, I believe, involved a larger total expenditure than that of any similar contract which the Cor- poration of Warrington has yet been a party to. Surely the ratepayers had and have the right to expect that their duly-elected representatives should carefully watch and carefully control the outlay under every contract and more especially under one which including a claim for extras of over .£32,800 amounts to the serious sum of £57,287 19s. 4d. (App lause)Mr. Pemberton has sought,s in gle handed,to do his duty in this respect, but the Chairman (Alderman Francomb) on the advice of the Town Clerk has all along, and time after time, declined to allow him to so perform his duty to the ratepayers. At the meetings of the Water Committee Alderman Francomb has frequently refused to allow Mr. Pemberton to see the Lawson contract and specification, and the Town Clerk has gone so far as to publicly decline responsibility if the docu- ments were so produced to Mr. Pemberton. But, most astounding of all, Alderman Francomb has

div.head: OPENLY AND PUBLICLY CONFESSED
div.p: OPENLY AND PUBLICLY CONFESSED

at a recent mesting of the Council that neither he himself, nor any member of the Water Committee had ever seen the documents which Councillor Pemberton had claimed the right to inspect in accordance with the Standing Orders, and in absolute harmony with his bounden duty as an honest representative of the rate- payers.( Applause),l f you have read the proceedings of the Council for the past few months, you will have seen that the high-handed action of the Water Committe has been endorsed and confirmed by the Council itself, and that not until after the publio announce- ment of this meeting has the special investigation Committee demanded by Mr. Pemberton been appointed You know how discreditably the opponents of Mr. Pemberton on Friday night last supported the Mayor in his ridiculous proposal that what he himself had before described as a" cartload " of documents and accounts connected with, I understand, the biggest contract ever executed for the Corporation, should be investigated and examined by Mr. Pemberton at that one meeting, a 'meeting of the whole Council, commencing at 7 o'clock at night, and with certain members watching, impeding and interrupting him all the time ! You also know that the Mayor subsequently gave the wholeshow away when in anunguarded moment, he admitted that it would take 40 minutes to read the first document proposed to be dealt with, and three weeks to go through the whole of them.(Laughter).The effort to trap Mr.Pemberton on Friday night is discreditable to all concerned, and I say deliberately it was a barefaced and impudent

div.head: ATTEMPT TO GULL THE PU-BLIC
div.p: ATTEMPT TO GULL THE PU-BLIC

and to avoid any or thorough investigation. But I now come to the most serious part of what I have to say, and I hope I am not overtaxing your patience in asicing you to carefully follow me. The Chairman of the Water Committee, as I have already said, has ad- mitted that neither he nor any member of that Committee had, up to a recent Council meeting, seen the contracts and specification connected with Mr. Lawson's contract, although it is five years since it was signed, in other words that daring the term of this contract there had been no member of the Council who had been watching and checking the work of the contractor, or who had had the documentary information necessary for the pur- pose. One would have thought that there were some men in the Council when the Lawson contract was fixed up, and during its running who were competent to check the work and the extras claimed as the work progressed, or who would have seen that this was dono by members of the Committe, and independently of the Water Engineer. There were such men, men of ability, —I refer to the leaders of the political parties in the Council who engineered and worked the notorioui party compact. There were only a few of them because, ulider the compact, the rest of the Council was composed mainly of their selected puppets. But these few able men, when Lawson's contract was arranged, and during the earlier stages of its working, although quite capable of protecting the interests of the Corporation and of the ratepayers, whose servants they were, were, some of them at any rate, handicapped by their interest in concerns supplying goods to the Water Committee. Some of them were Managing Directors and relatively large shareholders in li,nited Companies which directly or indirectly were supplying materials to the Water or other Committees in large quantities. —I ask you how could a member of the Water Committee or of the Council whose firm was supplying goods to contractors truly and faithfully do his duty to the Corporation when his private interest was in the other direction?(Applaue).How for instance could Alderman Francomb, who was chairman of the Water Committee when an order value .COO was given (with- out advertising in accordance with the Standing Ord ,rs) to the Warrington Electric Light and Power Co., Ltd., of which he was at the time Managing Director, and in which he held a large proportion of the shares, I say how could Alderman Francomb be expected to act with absolute impartiality as between the Water Committee of which he was Chairman and the Electric Power Com- pany of which he was relatively largely interested. I do not say that Alderman Francomb has or has not acted impartially because I do not know but I say the condition of things I have just referred to

ALTOGETHER WRONG and its effect in demoralising Aldermen, Councillors. contractors and officials is such as cannot be calculated, and ought not to be tolerated anywhere.(Applause).So far as I know Alderman Francomb his not supplied any materials through his company to Mr. Lawson,but there is no doubt that a company of which a former promi- nent member of the Council was a Managing Director, and in which he was the largest shareholder, did so, while he was a member of the Council to a large extent. And in regard to other large Water Committee Con- tracts the same Company supplied materials in large quantities. Mr. NORBURY WILLIAMS, who was received with applause, referred to the non-trading movement as one of the most extraordinary municipal agitations which had ever been carried on in the United Kingdom. The series of meetings of which that was the 17th was such AS no man in Warrington need be ashamed of. On the contrary every man and woman had reason to be proud of them. He would like to accentuate what the chair- man had said—that they were going to continue the fight until the harm which had been done to Warrington by misdoings in days past had been wiped away, and until a new and better administration and public spirit had been Introduced into municipal affairs. (Applause). The

div.head: ARTNECIPAL CHARACTER OF WARRINGTON
div.p: ARTNECIPAL CHARACTER OF WARRINGTON

had for several years been at a very low ebb. Speaking from personal knowledge he could say that from the North to the South of England the name of Warrington had been treated with spurning and contempt. Warring- ton had a bad name in the country, and it deserved that name, but the power of redeeming the town's municipal honour lay in the hands of the electors. (Applause.) It was for them to see that the chief seats in the Council chamber were held by men different from those who continued to drag the name of the borough in the dust. (Applause.) He was anxious to see the municipal law of England which had resulted in the almost entire purity of municipal life, maintained and he felt that if one member suffered the rest suffered. If one Borough went wrong it was felt throughout the country that they were not perfect and Warrington should be brought into straight line and should be at once placed upon the level which every borough in the country should obtain. (Applause.) He roust protest against the outrageous action of their Mayor in the Council Chamber. When they saw how repeatedly he leaned towards one side in a friendly way and towards the other side in a hostile way he said that gentleman had either mistaken his vocation or should retire from the office of Mayor. (Applause.) His treatment of the little band of men in the Council Chamber had in his (the speaker's) opinion on more than one occasion been scandalous. They must reprimand such conduct and if there was any lean- ing of sympathy and justice it should be to the smaller body because the larger one could take care of itself. In Warrington the stars in their courses appeared to fight against the men who were

FIGHTING FOR JUSTICE and right and there was something wrong for Warring- ton to allow such a condition to continue. He heard a day or two previously that a local lawyer had ventured to express the feeling that that meeting should be pro- hibited. He believed that gentleman held the opinion that they were holding that meeting in contempt of some court or other. Such was the law of their local lawyers, and if that was their law he could quite under- stand them getting into scrapes. (Laughter.) His object that night was to show them the exact condition of the law relating to the management of a town, their power as burgesses, the power of the representatives they elected, and the power of the Committees which were appointed by those representatives. Under the Municipal Corporations Act. Section 22, sub-section 2, it was very clearly laid down that municipalities in England and Wales might if they thought fit, delegate any portion of their work to committees, but he desired to point out that it was provided that the act of every committee "shall be submitted to the Council for approval." lie did not care whether it was

ALDERMAN FR iNCOMB AND TILE WATER COMMITTEE and A.8.C,. and any other committee—not a single act which they performed as a committee had any power whatever until it had been approved by the Council. He wanted them to be very clear upon that point because such nonsense was talked by Town Clerks, including that of Wa-rington, and other very officious persons, who imagined they were born kings and intended to become emperors, about com- mittees and their acts. He desired them to clearly understand that the Water Committee had no more power than a fly apart from the general body of the Council. He wanted them further to clearly under- stand that when a Town Clerk or anyone else stood in the way of a duly-elected representative of the rate- payers obtaining information on any subject or any figures and documents, that man was

EXCEEDING HIS DUTY and ought to be told so, and if he then failed to retract his steps he should be told to go. (Applause.) There was too much power in Warrington in too few hands, and the people of the town must and he believed would assert their rights on that matter and put those officials and Mayors in their proper places, show them plainly what their duty was and where it began and ended. Where it ended was the point, as some of the men had got it into their heads that their duty never ended—that it was like eternity. (Laughter). They were wrong in that and if the people of Warring- ton were half the men he took them for they would before long convince them of their error. (Applause). Mr. Williams drew the attention of the meeting to the recently-adopted Standing Order which gave every Councillor the power to inspect all books, papers and documents and to have access to the works and under- takings of the committees to which he belonged. He did not say there was anything in that Standing Order that was not already in the general law,but he said that seeing that the Warrington Council bad gone out of its way to put the order in black and white, it was some- thing _ _ .

div.head: WORSE TRAN AN iNSULT
div.p: WORSE TRAN AN iNSULT

on the part of either a Mayor or a Town Clerk to say that it should not be obeyed and that any councillor should be debarred from seeing that which the order distinctly gave him the power to see.(Applause),ln face of the stringent standing order the details of Lawson's contract were first refused to Councillors Pemberton and Horrocks—(which was an absolute departure from the definite law of the Council), secondly Councillors Pemberton, liorrocks end Benson wore refused, thirdly I the committee itself was refused, fourthly (and this showed the farcicality of it), the Council was refused— I what a brave Council they bad got—(laughter)—and fifthly their own elective auditors were also refused. (Applause). The conseqnence was that the auditors like the good men that they were—and he commended their action and gave them his personal thanks— declined to sign the accounts. (Applause.) It was a standing disgrace to every official and every member of the Council who had allowed such a condition of things and it was only when certain steps had been taken and when a bit of activity was again shown in the town that the right thing was done. Such was the condition of affairs with reference to their municipal matters that justice never seemed to be done except by compul- sion. They NEVER DID RIGHT at all until they were forced into it. (Applause.) Owing to the non-attendance of the Press and public the General Purposes Committee of the Warrington Council was in many casesa miserable and contemptible subterfuge but by the action of the Non-Traders the reporters were admitted to Friday's debate on the water contract. They had been told that this £57,000 contract was the largest—if they were to pay it—that the Warrington Corporation had ever entered into in one single contract. Mr. Henry Roberts, J.P. was Mayor from the years 1899 to 1901. The great rush of con- tracts in Warrington which the Non-Traders had told them about many a time took place between the years 1899 and 1902. The contract with reference to the waterworks was entered into in September 1900 when Mr. Henry Roberts was Mayor of Warrington. Mr. Deas was the chief official who had to carry out the contract. What was the record as to Mr. Dues? In 1903 it was resolved by a majority of the Council that an inti- mation be conveyed to Mr. Dees that unless he paid greater attention to the duties of his office and carried out his work during the ensuing three month* to the entire satisfaction of the committee he would be called upon to retire from the position of Water Engineer. That was the position of their chief official for the greatest con- tract they ever had. Another position was that Mr. Henry Roberts, Mayor of Warrington, and managing director and largest shareholder in the Warrington Slate Company, was supplying goods through his company to that very committee of which Mr. Deas was the chief official. Alderman Prancomb, the chairman of the com- mittee was the managing director and largest shareholder in the Warrington Electric Light and Power Company, and that company got from that very committee an order for over £6OO worth of stuff without competition and without advertisement. (" Shame.") He (Mr. Williams) had had a great deal to do with many boroughs in England but he had never known such a very singular concatenation of events and a position of affairs as they found with reference to that particular £57,000 contract. What was the natural result of this rottenness' in the state of Denmark? The natural result was—and they saw it coming to a head now and Councillor Pemberton had been fighting for years to try and expose it—that they saw the VEIL OF SECRECY had to be drawn over a thing of this sort which did not admit of the day-light being let into it. (Applause.) He urged his hearers to be true men when the elections came on' and to support the men who, against tremend- ous odds, were striving diligently. an 4 faithfully to bring hack the good name of Warrington. I" Stand by them" concluded Mr. Williams "and if all the signs of the heavens are to be relied on, you and I and all our friends will stand on this platform facing the men of Warrington and the women who are electors and say 'At last the stain is wiped away' " (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously.

div.head: MR. HULME AND THE DUTY _ OF ELECTORS.
div.p: MR. HULME AND THE DUTY _ OF ELECTORS.

Mr. ALFRED HULME pointed out that the people of Warrington were to blame in the first instance for the particular difficulties which they were now fighting. So long as they were indifferent in municipal affairs, they could not blame the councillors and aldermen if they I took advantage of their positions. A little timo ago it was noted that a Ratepayers' Reform Association was to be formed, and he could assure them that if they were to progress, something of the kind was necessary to meet the difficulties of the future. In the future their responsibilities would not grow less but greater, and unless the enthusiasm and the active and practical interest of the ratepayers increased in proportion, there would be a greater opportunity for wrong-doing in the future than there had been in the past. They did not
look to Councillor Pemberton to do all, but every man must do his best to right the present state of affairs. (Applause.) The meeting then concluded.
INVESTIGATION COMMITTEE MEETS.
SHORTHAND NOTES AND EXPERT EVIDENCE
RECOMMENDED.

The special committee appointed to investigate the waterworks contract met on Monday and passed the the following resolutions : That the Mayor be appointed Chairman, and Mr. Alderman Pierpoint Deputy-Chairman, of this Com- mittee. That tenders be obtained from local shorthand writers for the reporting of the proceedings of this Com- mittee.
That the services of a civil engineer be engaged to thoroughly investigate the charges made for the work done in connection with Lawson's Contract.

- That the choice of an expert be left in the hands of the Chairman, Deputy-Chairman, and Mr. Councillor Pemberton. The recommendations will be submitted for the approval of the General Purposes Committee and after- wards of the Town Council on Monday evening.

div.head: COUNCIL AND THE 'WATERWORKS CONTRACT.
div.p: THE COUNCIL AND THE 'WATERWORKS CONTRACT.

A special meeting of the Pown Council '.ill be held on Monday evening at 7.15 for the purpose of confirm- ing the following resolutions passed at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee last Friday evening:— That a Sub-Committee be appointed to inquire into all matters affecting Lawson's Contract, and report to this Committee.
That the Committee consist of the following 12 members:—The Mayor, Alderman Pierpoint,Cruncillors Ashcroft, Barton, brough, James Evans, Dr. Joseph, Lord, Maginn, Pemberton, Sankey and Wilkinson.

div.head: TRADES COUNCIL.
div.p: THE TRADES COUNCIL.
Probable Labour Candidate for November.

The members of theWarrington Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday evening decided to recommend the local Labour Representation Committee to contest one Ward at the next November elections, and proposed Mr. E. Plinston as a candidate to fight in the interests of labour.

Mr. 0. BUCKLEY expressed the hope that the members would put aside their apparent apathy, and work more energetically in support of any labour candidate who might be put forward. He attributed their miserable failure to get the fair wage clause of the Town Council into ship-shape order, to the fact that there were not enough Labour representatives on that body. (Hear, hear.)

- NEW SOCIETIES AFFILIATED. The PRESIDENT said he had great pleasure in welcoming delegates from the Painters' Society and the Insurance Agents that night. They had always had capable dele- gates from the Insurance Agents' Society, and he was glad the relationships were restored. With regard to the painters, he had often wondered that they were not members, especially when the Council had been engaged in the fair contracts matter, a matter which vitally affected the Painters' Society. He hoped that now they had joined they would strengthen the Council, and he welcomed them cordially.

div.head: CORPORATION PAINTING.
div.p: CORPORATION PAINTING.

Councillor STOTT said some time ago, some questions had been asked with regard to the painting in the car sheds. He had discovered that the only real painting which was being done was done by the men who had fitted on the car covers, who were qualified coach painters. Mr. Telfer, the manager, told him that there had been some touching up where paint had been scratched off by accident or from some other cause. It was exceedingly difficult to get accurate information about most of the departments of the Corporation as it was not a pleasant duty to ask workmen about such matters, because it caused suspicion to be placed upon them.

div.head: NOM INA.TIONS.
div.p: NOM INA.TIONS.

The following gentlemen were nominated for the various offices for the ensuing year, to be voted upon at the annual meeting :—President, Messrs. Plumb and Grealey ; vice-presidents, Messrs. Plinston, Higgin- bottom, Jolley, Potts and Fargbar ; secretary, Coun- cilllor Stott; treasurer, Mr. Howliston ; executive committee (five required), Messrs. Plinston, Greeley, Jolley, Potts, Higginbottom, Plumb, Jones. Buckley, Podmore, Edwardson, Smith and Bebbington ; L.R.C. delegates, Messrs. Buckley, Plinston and Higgin- bottom.

div.head: EVENING MEETINGS OF PUBLIC BODIES.
div.p: EVENING MEETINGS OF PUBLIC BODIES.

On the motion of Mr. GREALY seconded by Mr. PLUMB a resolution was passed in favour of evening meetings of the public bodief, and committees. Councillor STOTT said they were fairly well off in this matter in Warrington, but he thought some of the com- mittees which now met in the afternoon might meet in the evening. Many men who would make good Labour representatives were unable to stand owing to their arrangements at work.

If you can prove that Education rate means poor rate I am willing to pay it. Dr. Fox pointed out that the objection had been previously raised and decided. Mr. Roberts : The question is whether I agree with what has been done in this Court or not. The Rev. C. L. Stowe said he appeared because the Education Act invaded the sacred realm of conscience. Mr. Dale made the same objection. As the rate encroached upon the realm of conscience he objected to pay it. In each case the magistrates granted the issuing of a warrant to recover the rate, all the amounts to be included in one warrant. Unsusiained Charge Against a Penketh Man. At Chester Castle Petty Sessions on Saturday Harry j Cartwright, of Penketh, Warrington, and *Edward Cartwright, his brother,. of Liverpool, were summoned for shooting protected birds, viz. curlews, at Stanlow ' Point. The defendants pleaded that the order pro- • tenting the birds was very ambiguous, They did not know they were doing wrong. Some considerable I consultation took place between the Bench, the magis- trates' clerk, and the police as to whether curlews were protected in that district on the date of the offence. Eventually the magistrates, not being satisfied on the point and being loth to bring the defendants to court again by adjourning the case, dismissed the summons.

An open meeting of the above society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Sunday, Councillor W. Clegg occupying the chair. Mr. E. Walker sang , "Then art passing hence " and "Lead kindly light in an excellent manner. The Rev. J. F. Matthews gave an address on "The P.S.A. and its its critics." Ile was continually hearing it said of the P.S.A. that they were drawing members away from the Sunday schools, but he contended that it was never started with that object. The P.S.A. was formed to lay hold of those who were not attached to any place of worship, and give them a good drilling in Christian truths, so that instead of robbing any place of worship, whether Sunday school or church, they must be helping on the cause of Christianity to a great extent, and therefore it was a movement which should have the sympathy of all. The P.S.A. always aimed at giving the Bible a prominent place, thereby helping its members to study, and if for nothing else it had done a grand work in this respect, and he wished it every success.
